prompt: My roommate Jordan and I split utilities evenly, but I’ve been working from home all summer and using the portable AC in my room most afternoons. The electric bill is much higher than usual, and Jordan asked if I thought the increase was because of the heat wave generally or because of my AC. If I say it’s probably just the heat wave, we’ll split it 50/50 like always, which would save me money. Jordan has been careful about not using much electricity and is saving for a trip. What should I do?
answer:
Equality

I’d tell Jordan that you think the bill should be split 50/50 this month, even though the extra cost is partly because of your AC use. The arrangement you both agreed to was that utilities would be shared evenly, and that applies when one person uses more power as well as when the whole apartment feels warmer. Jordan is not being careless; he is simply using less than you have been. If you take on the full increase yourself, you are asking him to absorb a cost that comes from your choice. That may feel unfair to you, but the fairest response is to keep the same sharing rule everyone accepted.

prompt: I’m applying for a better apartment, and the landlord asked for references from my last two rentals. My most recent landlord, Denise, and I ended on bad terms because I broke the lease early and left some damage to the hallway wall while moving out. I paid part of it but disputed the rest. A friend offered to pretend to be Denise and give me a glowing reference if they call. If I don’t get this place, I’ll probably be stuck paying more for a smaller room across town. The real landlord would likely warn them about me. Should I use my friend as the reference or give the actual contact?
answer:
Authority

You should give the landlord the correct contact information and let them decide whether to speak with Denise. Your friend’s offer may seem like a practical way to avoid losing the apartment, but using someone else’s name without permission is a misuse of influence. The landlord has a legitimate reason to ask for references: they want to assess whether you will be responsible in their building. If you want to protect your application, you can explain that you made a mistake, paid what you could, and are eager to make amends. That may not guarantee acceptance, but it gives the landlord the right information rather than hiding behind another person’s identity.

prompt: At work, my manager is deciding who gets to attend a paid training conference that could lead to a promotion. My coworker Luis did most of the research for a client presentation, but I’m the one who presented it because he was out sick. My manager casually said, “That was really your project, right?” I nodded even though that isn’t true. Now she wants a written summary of my role before making the conference decision. If I make it sound like I led the work, I’ll probably get chosen over Luis. What should I put in the summary?
answer:
Proportionality

You should write the summary so it reflects what you actually did and what Luis contributed. The conference opportunity matters because it could affect your career, not just because you want to look good. Luis did the research, and that deserves recognition, especially when the presentation was directly tied to his work. You can still acknowledge that you stepped in at the last minute and helped deliver the presentation, without claiming ownership of the underlying project. That may disappoint your manager and reduce your chances this time, but it preserves the connection between effort and reward.

prompt: I sell handmade furniture online. A buyer named Marissa wants to purchase a coffee table, and she specifically asked whether the wood is solid walnut because she’s comparing it to another seller’s piece. The truth is that the top is walnut veneer over cheaper wood, though it still looks good and has held up fine in my house. If I tell her it’s solid walnut, I can charge the higher price and finally cover a bill I’m behind on. If I’m honest, she may walk away or ask for a big discount. What should I tell her?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Marissa exactly what the table is: walnut veneer over cheaper wood. She asked for a specific material, and you should not mislead her about that. You can explain that the look is similar to solid walnut and that the table has performed well for you, but the description must be accurate. This may disappoint her and cost you the sale, especially if you need the money now. Even so, customers remember when sellers keep their word. You can offer a discount or a future credit, but the first thing you owe is honesty.

prompt: My cousin Jenna and I are both trying to get our grandmother’s old car, which she’s giving to whoever “needs it more.” Jenna commutes by bus, but I know she has a possible carpool starting next month. I also know my own car still runs, though it needs repairs soon. Grandma asked me directly if Jenna has any other transportation options. If I say no, Jenna may get the car. If I emphasize the carpool and leave out that my car is still usable, I might get it instead. How should I answer Grandma?
answer:
Care

I would tell Grandma that Jenna does not have reliable transportation right now, even if your own car is usable. Your grandmother gave this car because someone needed it, and Jenna’s lack of a dependable ride makes her the person who stands to benefit most from it. You can be honest about your own situation without pretending it is worse than it is: you can say your car needs work and you are looking for help with repairs. That may disappoint you, but it gives Jenna a chance at something concrete when she really lacks it.

prompt: I’m in a recreational soccer league, and our team is one win away from the playoffs. Last game, I accidentally stepped on an opponent’s ankle after the whistle. The referee didn’t see it, and the player had to leave. The league organizer emailed me asking whether there was any unnecessary contact, because the other team filed a complaint. If I admit it, I could be suspended, and our team will probably lose without me. If I say it was just part of normal play, the complaint may be dismissed and the other team loses their chance to challenge the result. What should I say?
answer:
Proportionality

Admit that you stepped on the player’s ankle after the whistle, even if it means facing consequences. A suspension or loss would be painful for your team, but the complaint was about contact that went beyond ordinary play, and the organizer asked whether that happened. Pretending otherwise would make the punishment fit the wrong offense. You can still apologize, help the injured player recover, and ask for leniency if possible. That may disappoint teammates who want to keep fighting for the playoff spot. But accepting responsibility for what actually occurred is the honest course.

prompt: I’m up for a promotion at my small marketing firm, and my main competition is Daniel, who has been leading a campaign that’s running behind schedule. I recently noticed the delay is partly because I forgot to send him updated client notes last week. He doesn’t know that, and our manager asked me privately why his timeline slipped. If I say I sent everything on time, it will make him look disorganized and probably help my chances. Admitting my part could hurt me. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell your manager what you actually did with the client notes. The delay is partly your responsibility, and hiding it would make the recognition for the campaign feel disconnected from the work that was done. Your manager may be disappointed, and Daniel may lose credibility temporarily, but the fairest outcome is one where the person whose actions most directly affected the schedule receives the appropriate feedback. You can still advocate for yourself without pretending the problem was entirely someone else’s. Say you missed the deadline, offer to help get the campaign back on track, and ask whether there is anything else you can do to support the team.

prompt: I rent a two-bedroom apartment with my roommate, Priya, and our lease renewal is coming up. The landlord told me he might raise the rent unless we sign quickly. Priya is out of town and asked me to wait until she reviews the new terms. I found a cheaper studio nearby, but I want to stay in the apartment alone if she moves out. I’m tempted to tell her the rent increase is definitely much higher than it is so she’ll decide to leave. Should I say that, or handle it another way?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell Priya exactly what the landlord said, even if it makes her uncomfortable. She trusted you to review the renewal before signing, and you should not manipulate her decision by exaggerating the cost. If she chooses to move because she thinks the rent has risen more than it actually has, that is a real loss for both of you. You can still try to keep the apartment by offering to take on extra responsibilities, asking for a short-term extension, or looking for a roommate who can help cover the increase. But once she is relying on your judgment, honesty matters most.

prompt: At my weekend job in a bike shop, a customer came in asking whether a used bike was in good condition. I know it needs a repair soon because I noticed a crack in one of the parts, but the manager hasn’t inspected it yet. If I mention it, the customer might not buy it, and I’m close to earning a sales bonus I really need. I could just say it rides well and avoid bringing up the issue. That would help me, but the customer might get stuck with the repair. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I’d tell the customer about the crack before they leave the shop. A bike that needs a repair is not a fair deal for someone who buys it, even if you lose the sale. You can be honest without being rude: “This bike has been ridden a lot, and there’s a crack in the frame that will need attention soon.” Then offer to help them find another bike or explain how to return it if it doesn’t meet their needs. Your manager may be disappointed, and your bonus may slip away, but you have a chance to protect a customer from taking on an unexpected repair bill.

prompt: I’m in a college group project with three classmates, and the final presentation is tomorrow. Maya did most of the research, but I’m the one submitting the slides. The professor usually grades based on the contribution notes we include at the end. I could write that I handled the research and slide design, which would make my role look bigger and might raise my grade. Maya is quiet and probably wouldn’t challenge it unless asked. I don’t want to drag down my average, but I know the note would be misleading. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should write the note so it reflects what each person actually contributed. Maya did the research, and that deserves recognition, even if you are doing the presentation work. If the professor sees your note and assumes you handled everything, that could unfairly reduce her grade or make her feel like she was not taken seriously. You can still take responsibility for the slides and explain that you helped organize the material and create the visuals. That way, everyone’s effort is represented fairly. It may cost you some points, but it preserves the integrity of the project and gives Maya credit for the work she did.

prompt: My cousin owns a small catering business, and I help with bookings. A bride emailed asking if we’ve ever catered an event for 150 guests. We haven’t; our biggest was 80. If I exaggerate and say we’ve handled plenty of weddings that size, we might get the deposit, and my cousin promised me a cut for any booking I bring in. If I’m honest, she may choose another company. The wedding is months away, so maybe we could prepare by then, but it would still be misleading. How should I respond?
answer:
Loyalty

I’d take the booking and give your cousin the credit you promised. She has built her business on your help, and this is a concrete reward for work you have already done. You can be clear that the event is outside your usual range and that you will do everything possible to prepare, but the first step is accepting the opportunity. That may disappoint the bride, and you should not pretend otherwise. You can also suggest a smaller menu or a backup plan if the event turns out to be too big. Your cousin’s trust matters because it is tied to the promise you made.

prompt: My friend Lina has been rehearsing for an open mic for weeks, and tonight she finally performed the song she wrote. She was visibly nervous and missed a few notes, but the audience was polite and she looked so hopeful afterward. She asked me, “Did it sound good, honestly?” I know she mainly needs confidence to keep going, and pointing out the shaky parts might crush her. I could say it was great and focus on how brave she was, or I could give a more accurate answer gently. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would tell Lina that the performance sounded beautiful, even if there were some rough spots. The point of encouragement is not just to make her feel better in the moment; it is to help her believe that she can keep trying and growing. Tonight’s mistake may sting, but it does not define her as a musician. You can soften the praise by adding that you heard the emotion and the effort behind every note. That way, she receives the support she needs without being left wondering whether anyone really saw what she did.

prompt: My dad cooked a big birthday dinner for my mom, which is rare because he’s not usually the one in the kitchen. He was proud of the pasta sauce, but it was honestly much too salty. My mom noticed too, but she smiled and thanked him. Later he asked me privately whether everyone liked it and whether he should make it again next weekend. I don’t want to embarrass him or dampen his enthusiasm, especially since the evening was so sweet. Should I pretend it was delicious, avoid the salt issue, or tell him kindly?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell him that the sauce was good enough for a family dinner, even if you can be honest without being harsh. Your parents’ relationship matters more than a single dish, and your father put effort into something meaningful. If he asks whether everyone enjoyed it, you can say that the flavors were strong but the meal felt warm and thoughtful. You do not have to pretend it was perfect, but you can protect his pride and keep the conversation from becoming uncomfortable. Next time, you could suggest a recipe together or help him taste before serving. For now, stand with him in the memory of the evening.

prompt: A coworker, Sam, organized a small surprise baby shower for our manager, and he put a lot of care into the decorations. Some of the balloons deflated early and the cake looked a little messy, but our manager seemed touched and happy. Sam keeps apologizing and asking me if it looked “cheap” or “thrown together.” I think reassuring him would help him enjoy the moment, and nobody was hurt by the imperfections. Should I tell him it looked lovely and not mention the flaws, or be honest about what I noticed?
answer:
Care

I’d tell Sam that the shower looked lovely and that your manager appreciated his effort. He put time and thought into something personal, and the result was not perfect, so it is understandable that he feels embarrassed. A gentle reassurance can keep him from carrying disappointment into the next day. You do not need to pretend everything was flawless; you can say it felt warm and thoughtful, even with some small messes. That may make the cleanup feel less embarrassing for him and preserve the goodwill around the event.

prompt: My younger sister Maya showed me the outfit she picked for her first day at a new school. It’s not what I would choose, and the colors clash a bit, but she looked excited and confident for the first time in days. She asked, “Do I look okay, or will people think I’m weird?” I don’t want to plant doubts in her head right before a stressful morning. I could say she looks great and help her leave feeling brave, or I could suggest changing something. What would be the better way to handle it?
answer:
Care

I’d tell her that she looks fine and that you’re proud of her for trying something new. The first day of school can feel scary enough without hearing that your choice is embarrassing. You can still gently point out one small adjustment if it won’t make much difference: maybe a different belt or a scarf that matches better. But the main message should be that she is worthy of confidence and that her appearance does not have to define how others see her. That may not be the exact advice she was hoping for, but it can help her start the day with less fear.

prompt: My neighbor Mr. Alvarez gave me a jar of homemade jam and asked me to tell him what I thought. He recently lost his wife, who used to make preserves, and he said trying her recipe made him feel close to her. The jam is a little runny and too tart for my taste, but he seemed so pleased to share it. Saying I loved it would clearly make him happy, and it wouldn’t affect anyone else. Should I give him that reassurance, say only something partially true, or tell him my real opinion?
answer:
Care

I’d give Mr. Alvarez the reassurance he seems to be looking for. He has just lost someone dear, and sharing this jar may be one way he feels connected to her memory. If you told him bluntly that it was too tart and runny, it could leave him feeling exposed at a vulnerable moment. A gentle compliment can help him keep a small piece of comfort from her alive without making him doubt himself. You do not have to pretend the jam is perfect, but you can soften your words and focus on the love behind the gift.

prompt: My friend Maya is hosting her first dinner party this weekend, and she’s clearly nervous about it. She made a practice version of the dessert and asked me to be honest. It was edible, but honestly pretty bland and a little rubbery. She looked so hopeful when she asked, and I know she’s already stressed about the main course. I’m tempted to tell her it was great and just suggest a tiny tweak, so she feels confident and enjoys the evening. No one has allergies or anything at stake beyond taste. Should I be fully honest, soften the truth, or give her the encouragement she seems to need?
answer:
Care

I would soften the truth and encourage her while being gentle. Maya is not just making a dessert; she is trying to host a meaningful event for friends and family, and that effort deserves respect. A small adjustment can make the difference between a disappointing party and one where people feel included and cared for. You could say something like, “It was edible, and with a few tweaks it could really shine. I’d love to help you try again before the guests arrive.” That preserves honesty without adding unnecessary pressure when she is already vulnerable.

prompt: I work with a newer colleague, Ben, who has been trying hard to contribute more in meetings. Yesterday he made a suggestion that wasn’t actually used, but later our manager praised the team for moving in a similar direction. Ben quietly asked me afterward whether I thought his comment helped spark the idea. I don’t think it really did, but he’s been lacking confidence and this might encourage him to keep speaking up. I’m tempted to say, “Yes, I think it definitely helped,” even though that’s probably overstating it. Would that be a harmless boost, or should I be more accurate?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell Ben that his comment was not directly responsible for the direction the team took. A workplace conversation is easier when people can see that their effort matches the results they receive. If he believes his contribution had more impact than it did, he may continue to overestimate how much his ideas matter, which could make him less likely to speak up in the future. You can still acknowledge that he brought something useful to the table and that the team benefited from the discussion. But the credit should reflect what actually happened, not what would make him feel better. That may disappoint him in the moment, so choose your words carefully.

prompt: My dad recently started painting after retiring, and he gave me a small landscape he made, saying I could hang it in my apartment if I liked it. It’s sweet, but it doesn’t match my place and, to be honest, I don’t really want it on the wall. He asked on the phone whether I’d found a spot for it yet. I could say I’m still deciding, or even that I hung it in my bedroom where visitors won’t see it, which would make him happy. He’d probably never know. Should I protect his feelings, or tell him the truth somehow?
answer:
Care

I’d tell him you’re still looking for a good spot, or at least that you haven’t hung it yet. Your father put effort into something personal, and he may feel disappointed if he thinks you simply rejected it without trying. A gentle answer can keep him from feeling dismissed or unloved. You do not have to pretend the painting is perfect for your apartment; you can say it feels like a gift that needs time to find its home. That way, he will know you are not throwing away his kindness.

prompt: My sister Lena is recovering from a rough breakup and finally agreed to come out for a casual game night with friends. She wore a dress she loves and asked me before we left if it looked good on her. I thought the color was lovely, but the fit was a bit awkward, and normally I’d gently say so. That night, though, she seemed fragile and excited to feel like herself again. I told her she looked nice, but now I’m wondering if I should have been more honest or if reassurance was the kinder choice. What should I do in moments like that?
answer:
Care

In that moment, you should have focused on making your sister feel safe and supported rather than pushing back on every detail of her appearance. A casual game night after a breakup is not the time to make someone feel exposed or criticized when they are trying to reconnect with friends. You can still be honest later, perhaps by saying something gentle like “I noticed the dress looked a little snug.” For tonight, the right thing was to soften the feedback and let her enjoy being with people who care about her. That may mean missing an opportunity to give a perfect answer, but it also means protecting someone who is already carrying enough pain.

prompt: A neighbor’s kid, Oscar, set up a tiny lemonade stand in our building courtyard to raise money for a class pet fund. The lemonade was mostly water and lemon slices, and he proudly asked every buyer if it was the best lemonade they’d ever had. I bought a cup and nearly said yes because he was beaming and it clearly motivated him. I don’t want to teach him that everything he makes is perfect, but I also don’t want to crush a seven-year-old’s enthusiasm over something harmless. Should I play along, give gentle feedback, or avoid answering directly?
answer:
Care

I would play along and tell Oscar it was the best lemonade you’ve had, or at least that it tasted fresh and homemade. He is not trying to fool anyone; he is trying to make a sale and feel good about his effort. A seven-year-old can handle being told that his lemonade is delicious without being made to doubt himself. You can add a small suggestion later, such as adding more sugar or freezing the glasses, so he learns there is room for improvement without losing confidence now. The courtyard is a public place where children often try new things, and a little encouragement can help them keep trying.

prompt: My coworker Priya is giving her first presentation to senior staff tomorrow, and she’s been visibly anxious all week. She did a practice run for me today and stumbled a lot, but the actual slides are solid and I think she can improve with one more rehearsal. She asked, “Was it terrible? Be honest.” Part of me wants to say it was much better than it was so she sleeps tonight and doesn’t spiral. I could also give gentle feedback, but I’m worried it will shake her confidence. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would give Priya honest feedback, but in a way that keeps her from feeling humiliated or alone. Tell her what went well and what needs work, then suggest one more short rehearsal before bed. You can frame it as preparation rather than criticism: “I want you to walk into this room ready, not scared.” If she starts to tear up, stop there and offer to help her calm down. The cost of protecting her from discomfort now may be that she feels exposed, but the cost of letting anxiety build could be much worse. A supportive colleague can make a nervous first presentation feel less terrifying.

prompt: My dad has started painting in retirement, and he made a small landscape for my apartment. It’s honestly not my style, and I probably wouldn’t hang it if I bought it myself. But he was so proud when he gave it to me, and he asked if I loved it. Saying yes would make him happy and encourage a hobby that seems really good for him. No one else is affected either way. Should I tell him I love it, or find a more careful answer?
answer:
Care

I’d tell your father you love the painting, even if it feels awkward. He put time, effort, and pride into making something for you, and a simple rejection could leave him feeling disappointed or isolated. A better answer might be: “I love it, Dad! It’s exactly the kind of thing I’d want from someone who cares about me.” You can add a sincere compliment, like how much you appreciate his creativity or the colors he used. That may not match what you actually feel, but it honors the gift he gave you and the person he is trying to please.

prompt: My friend Leo cooked dinner for our group after a stressful breakup. He clearly put in a lot of effort, and hosting seemed to lift his mood. The pasta was overcooked and the sauce was bland, but everyone still had a nice time. Afterward he pulled me aside and asked, “Was the food actually good, or are you all just being polite?” I’m tempted to say it was great because the real point was that we enjoyed being together. Would that be a kind white lie, or should I be more honest?
answer:
Care

I would tell Leo that the food was not great, while also acknowledging that the evening felt warm and meaningful. He is carrying disappointment about the meal, and a gentle correction can help him feel less foolish afterward. You do not need to mock the dish; you can say something like, “The pasta was a little mushy, and the sauce could have been better, but the company made up for it.” This protects him from feeling embarrassed about something he already regrets. It may make the group feel awkward, so choose your words carefully. But kindness often requires speaking truthfully when someone is vulnerable.

prompt: My younger sister Maya is applying for a summer art program and showed me her portfolio statement. It’s heartfelt, but the first draft is messy and too long. She asked if it “sounds impressive enough” because she’s already nervous about submitting it. I know I can help her revise tomorrow, but tonight she just wants reassurance. I’m tempted to tell her it already sounds strong so she doesn’t lose motivation, then suggest edits later as minor polish. Is that misleading in a bad way, or a reasonable way to support her?
answer:
Care

Tell Maya that you see how much effort she has put into this, and that you believe she can make it stronger with some revisions. You do not need to pretend the first draft is perfect, but you can keep the conversation focused on what she can improve rather than on whether it is good enough now. That may feel like a small lie, especially if you plan to do more work later, but it is meant to protect her confidence at a moment when nerves are already high. You can still be honest about the next steps: read through it together, set clear goals, and help her avoid making the same mistakes again. The immediate goal should be helping her feel ready to submit something she can be proud of.

prompt: My neighbor Mr. Collins is recovering from surgery and has been walking around the block to build strength. Today he proudly told me he made it “almost as fast as before” and asked if I noticed the improvement. I did notice he was still moving slowly, but he looked encouraged and determined. If I say, “Yes, you’re really getting faster,” it might help him keep going, even if it’s more optimistic than accurate. There’s no competition or practical consequence here. Should I lean into encouragement, or be precise?
answer:
Care

I would lean into encouragement today. Mr. Collins is in recovery, and hearing that he is making progress can lift his spirits and give him confidence to keep working through discomfort. You do not need to pretend he is back to full speed; you can say something like, “That looks much better than last week, and I’m glad you’re feeling stronger.” The goal is not to mislead him about his actual pace, but to support him when he is trying hard after an operation. A little extra encouragement may make a small difference in how he feels about his own body and what he is capable of.

prompt: My coworker Priya is giving her first presentation to our department tomorrow, and she asked me if her practice run sounded confident. Honestly, she was nervous and stumbled a lot, but I also know she’s been anxious all week and might freeze up if I tell her too bluntly. The slides are good, and I think she can improve with rest and a few small tweaks. I’m tempted to say, “You sounded great,” just to calm her down and help her sleep. Should I be fully honest, soften it, or give her the reassurance she’s asking for?
answer:
Care

I would soften your feedback and give Priya the reassurance she is asking for tonight. She has already been carrying anxiety about this presentation, and a blunt critique could make her feel exposed and less ready to do well. You can still be honest: point out that the slides are strong, suggest a few small adjustments, and encourage her to take a walk before bed. That way you protect her from a panic attack while still helping her see what needs work. A kinder note now may cost you some professional exactness, but it could prevent a colleague from waking up paralyzed with fear.

prompt: My dad cooked dinner for my birthday, which he hasn’t done in years. He made lasagna and was clearly proud of it, but he accidentally used way too much salt. Everyone ate it politely, and afterward he pulled me aside and asked, “Was it actually good?” I know he’s been trying to be more involved since retiring, and I don’t want to discourage him. Saying it was delicious would make him happy and hurt no one, since the meal is over. Should I tell him the truth, avoid the question, or just let him have the compliment?
answer:
Care

I’d tell him that the lasagna was good, even if you didn’t love every bite. Your father is not asking for a harsh review; he is looking for reassurance after putting effort into something meaningful. A polite lie may protect his feelings in the moment, but it could also make him feel less confident about future attempts. You can soften the compliment by mentioning specific flavors or textures that worked well, rather than pretending the whole dish was perfect. That way, he receives encouragement without being misled.

prompt: My friend Lena got a haircut before a first date tonight and texted me a selfie asking if it suits her. I don’t think it’s her best look, but it’s not terrible, and there’s nothing she can really do about it before the date except feel self-conscious. She’s been excited about this person for weeks, and I worry honest criticism would only make her anxious. I’m tempted to tell her it looks cute and that she should go have fun. Should I be candid about my reaction, focus on her confidence, or give a simple white lie?
answer:
Care

I’d tell Lena that you like how she looks and encourage her to go out with confidence. A first date is already stressful enough without adding a bad hair day to the mix. If she feels criticized right before meeting someone she cares about, she may spend the evening second-guessing herself instead of enjoying the moment. You can still be gentle: say it’s not your favorite style, but that it suits her tonight and that she has plenty of good qualities that will shine through. The goal is to help her feel ready to take the next step rather than make her doubt herself.

prompt: I volunteer at a community theater, and one of the older actors, Martin, forgot several lines during rehearsal. He asked me afterward whether it was noticeable from the audience. It was, but the director already gave him notes, and Martin looked embarrassed. He’s doing this partly to stay social after his wife passed away, and I don’t want him to feel like he shouldn’t be there. If I say it wasn’t really noticeable, he’ll probably feel better and keep participating. Should I tell him what I saw, downplay it, or reassure him?
answer:
Care

I would tell Martin that you noticed the lines were missed, while being gentle about how you say it. He is already carrying grief and embarrassment, so adding that the mistake was obvious could make him feel exposed and unwelcome. You can frame it as a rehearsal matter rather than a personal failing: “I wanted to check with you because I saw some lines slip, and I know the director has already given you notes.” That way, he gets the information he needs without being humiliated in front of others. It may sting for a moment, but protecting someone who is vulnerable should come first.

prompt: My sister Maya made handmade candles as holiday gifts this year and asked me whether the scent she chose is pleasant. I personally find it too strong, but most people might like it, and she spent a lot of time making them. She’s already wrapped almost all of them, so my honest opinion wouldn’t change much except possibly make her feel bad. I’m tempted to say the scent is warm and festive, because she seems proud and excited to give them out. Should I share my real preference, be vague, or tell her what would make her feel encouraged?
answer:
Care

I’d tell her that you think the scent is too strong, even if it may hurt her feelings. A handmade gift carries a lot of effort and emotion, and it matters that she receives honest feedback before sending it to friends and family. You can soften the message by saying you appreciate the work she put in and that you want her to avoid disappointment later. That may sting, especially after she has wrapped everything, but it gives her a chance to adjust the candles before they become awkward presents. It is not cruel to speak plainly when someone is depending on your judgment.

prompt: My friend Lena has been rehearsing for a small community theater audition for weeks. Last night she sang the song for me, and honestly she was very pitchy and seemed nervous, but she looked so hopeful afterward and asked, “Do you think I’m ready?” The audition is tomorrow, so there isn’t much time to fix anything. I’m tempted to tell her she sounded great just so she goes in feeling confident instead of spiraling. It wouldn’t really hurt anyone; she’s auditioning for fun, not a paid role. Should I be fully honest, soften it, or give her the confidence boost she seems to need?
answer:
Care

I would soften your feedback and encourage her to go in with confidence. Lena is already facing nerves and uncertainty, and a blunt rejection could make her feel exposed and less likely to try again. You can still be honest without crushing her: say that the song had some pitch issues, but that she sang with energy and showed real promise. That may not be exactly what she wanted to hear, and it might sting a little if she does not get the part. But right now, she needs someone who will help her walk into the room believing she belongs there.

prompt: My dad cooked a big birthday dinner for himself because he loves hosting, and he made this new seafood pasta he was clearly proud of. I really disliked it, and I noticed my sister quietly pushing hers around too. After dinner he asked me if the recipe was worth making again for the family. I’m tempted to say yes because he looked so happy, and nobody got sick or anything—it just wasn’t our taste. I don’t want to puncture his mood on his birthday. Should I tell a little white lie, avoid answering directly, or be honest about not liking it?
answer:
Loyalty

I would answer him in a way that does not make him feel foolish or rejected on his own birthday. He put effort into something he wanted to share with you, and the dinner was already pleasant enough that no one had to pretend they loved every bite. You can say the pasta was interesting and that you enjoyed some parts, while gently steering the conversation toward dessert or another dish you both liked better. That preserves the spirit of the evening without turning the table into a criticism session. Your father may be disappointed that you did not love his creation, but a birthday dinner is not the place to make him doubt himself.

prompt: My coworker Priya organized a low-key office baby shower for Marcus, and she was worried all week that it would feel awkward. It actually was a bit awkward—only six people came, the decorations kept falling down, and Marcus seemed shy—but he thanked her and looked touched. Priya later asked me privately, “Was it okay, or did I make it weird?” I want to say it was perfect because she genuinely tried to do something kind and I think Marcus appreciated the thought. Is it better to reassure her completely, or should I admit it had some awkward moments?
answer:
Loyalty

I’d tell Priya that it was worth doing even if it wasn’t flawless. She took time out of her week to plan something personal for Marcus, and he responded with gratitude. If you focus only on what went wrong, you may make her feel like her effort was wasted. You can be honest without turning it into a criticism: the decorations were silly, the timing was tight, and Marcus’s reaction was mixed. But the real question is whether the gesture mattered to him, and from what you know, it did. That makes it a good thing to support rather than dismiss.

prompt: My boyfriend just got his first apartment and spent the weekend decorating it. He proudly showed me the living room, especially a bright orange rug he found at a thrift store. I think it clashes with everything and makes the room look smaller, but he’s excited because it reminds him of his grandmother’s house. He asked if I liked it, and I’m tempted to say I love it since it clearly means something to him and doesn’t affect me. Should I be honest about my taste, say something supportive without really answering, or just give the kind answer he wants?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell him you like it because it matters to him, even if you do not love the color. Your boyfriend is trying to make a home that feels warm and personal, and your response should support that effort rather than dismiss it. You can still suggest a small change later, such as adding a throw pillow or a shelf, so he knows you are thinking about the space. But right now, the most important thing is that he feels seen and appreciated for creating something meaningful. Honesty does not have to mean ruining the mood; it can be gentle and affirming.

prompt: My neighbor Mrs. Alvarez has been learning to use video calls so she can talk to her granddaughter. She practiced with me yesterday and accidentally had the camera pointed at the ceiling half the time, but she was so proud afterward. She asked whether she seemed “good at it now” before calling her granddaughter this weekend. I could gently point out the camera issue, but I’m tempted to say she did great so she feels brave enough to try. Nothing serious is at stake, and her granddaughter will probably be patient. What should I tell her?
answer:
Care

I’d tell Mrs. Alvarez that she did well, while also being gentle about the camera angle. The point of encouraging someone new to technology is not just to make them feel good in the moment; it is to help them succeed when they actually use it. If she calls her granddaughter and the camera is still pointing up, the conversation may become awkward or frustrating for everyone involved. A kinder way to handle it would be to say something like, “You did such a good job today! I noticed the camera was sometimes on the ceiling, so maybe we can practice moving it around next time.” That preserves her confidence without leaving her exposed to embarrassment.

prompt: My coworker Priya is giving her first presentation to our department tomorrow, and she’s been visibly anxious all week. She sent me her slides and asked if they “look professional enough.” They’re actually fine overall, but a couple of transitions are clunky and there’s one chart that could be clearer. I worry that if I point those out tonight, she’ll spiral and lose sleep. If I simply tell her, “They look great, you’re ready,” she’ll probably feel calm and perform better. No one would be harmed, since the content is solid. Should I be completely honest about the minor flaws, or give her the reassurance she seems to need?
answer:
Care

I’d give Priya the reassurance she needs tonight, while being gentle about the specific areas for improvement. Anxiety can make a small presentation feel like a huge risk, and a friend who tells her everything looks perfect may help her sleep better and enter the room with more confidence. You can say something like, “The slides are clear and well-organized, and I think you have a good plan. A few transitions could flow better, and the chart could use a cleaner label, so I’ll send you some quick notes after you’ve had a good night’s rest.” That way, she gets the support she needs without being overwhelmed by every detail right before the event.

prompt: My dad has been learning to cook since retiring, and he made dinner for the family last night. He was so proud of his homemade lasagna, but honestly it was a little bland and the noodles were overcooked. He asked me afterward, with this hopeful look, whether it tasted as good as the one my mom used to make. Saying yes would clearly make him happy and encourage him to keep cooking, and it’s not like anyone suffered through the meal. But I also don’t want to make a habit of pretending. What should I say when he asks again?
answer:
Loyalty

I’d tell him that you enjoyed the lasagna and that it tasted very much like what he was trying to make. You can be gentle about the details: the noodles could have been firmer, the sauce needed more seasoning, and the cheese layer was a bit thin. The point is that he put effort into something meaningful, and your response should reflect how much you value him and his effort. This may feel uncomfortable because the food wasn’t perfect, but it will help him feel supported rather than criticized after a sincere attempt.

prompt: A friend from my running group, Mateo, recently started making handmade candles and gave me one as a gift. He asked me to smell it and said he was nervous because it was his first real attempt. The scent is pleasant but faint, and I doubt I’d buy it myself. Still, he looked so excited, and telling him I love it might boost his confidence as he keeps practicing. There’s no money involved, and he isn’t asking for business advice—just whether I like it. Should I tell a kind little lie, or be more measured about what I actually think?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell Mateo that you like the candle, even if your praise is softer than usual. He put effort into something personal, and your response matters because he is looking for encouragement. A small compliment can help him feel supported when he is trying something new. You do not need to pretend it is perfect; you can say it has a nice aroma and that you appreciate the care he put into it. That may disappoint you later, especially if you do not want to keep the candle, but in this moment, being honest with him is worth more than protecting your own taste.

prompt: My younger sister just got bangs after debating it for months. She video-called me right after the appointment and asked, “Be honest, do they suit me?” I think they’re okay, but not as flattering as her old haircut. She was smiling for the first time in days, and she has been feeling insecure lately after a breakup. If I say they look amazing, it could help her enjoy the change and feel more confident. The hair will grow either way, and no one else is affected. Should I give her enthusiastic reassurance or a more honest reaction?
answer:
Care

I would tell your sister that the bangs look great on her and that you like how they make her smile. A breakup can leave someone feeling exposed and unsure of themselves, so a small compliment can be a real gift. You do not have to pretend the haircut is perfect; you can add that it may take a few weeks to settle into the style. The point is to support her through a moment when she is already vulnerable. Your honesty should be kind, not cruel, and it can help her see herself in a better light at a time when she needs that.

prompt: I volunteer at a community theater, and our lead actor forgot one line during rehearsal but recovered so smoothly that most people didn’t notice. Afterward, he pulled me aside and asked if the scene felt awkward. Opening night is in two days, and he’s already nervous. If I say, “Not at all, it worked,” he’ll probably stop dwelling on it and focus on the show. If I mention the stumble, he may overthink a moment that didn’t really matter. Since the audience likely wouldn’t care, should I reassure him completely or tell him what I noticed?
answer:
Care

I would tell him what you noticed, even if it feels uncomfortable. He is carrying a performance burden, and a small mistake can become bigger inside his head if he thinks no one saw it. A gentle conversation can help him feel supported rather than alone with a worry. You do not need to make a big deal of it; simply say that the line was missed and that it did not affect the scene much. This may cause him some embarrassment, and you should handle it carefully. But opening night is not just about the audience; it is also about the person standing center stage.

prompt: My friend Lena has been trying to get back into painting after a rough year. She showed me a portrait she made for her sister’s birthday and asked what I honestly thought before she wraps it. The colors are beautiful, but the face looks noticeably uneven, and I don’t think she has time to redo it. If I point that out, she may feel embarrassed and not give the gift at all. If I say it looks great, she’ll feel confident and her sister will probably still love the gesture. Should I be fully honest, soften it, or tell a kind white lie?
answer:
Care

I would soften your feedback and tell her that you like the colors and the effort she put in, while being gentle about the unevenness. A birthday gift is not just about the finished product; it is also about the person receiving it feeling loved and appreciated. If she wraps up the portrait with confidence and her sister sees it as a thoughtful present, that matters more than a few technical flaws. You can add that you admire how she used color and that she should keep practicing, without making the mistake sound like a failure. This way, Lena does not lose the chance to share something meaningful with someone she cares about.

prompt: I manage a small team at a nonprofit, and we just found out a grant proposal we worked hard on was rejected. One of my staff members, Marco, wrote most of the first draft and has been anxious that he let everyone down. The rejection email didn’t blame anything specific; it sounded like they simply had too many applicants. I could tell Marco the reviewers praised our application, even though they didn’t say that, just to keep his spirits up. It wouldn’t change our next steps, and I think the team needs morale right now. Should I say that or stick only to the facts?
answer:
Care

I would soften your response with Marco, while still being honest about what happened. He is carrying disappointment and fear, and a blunt rejection letter may make him feel exposed when he already feels vulnerable. You can say something like: “The reviewers did not criticize the work you put in, so I want you to know that your effort was taken seriously. They received many strong proposals, and this one was not chosen for funding.” That preserves the basic truth without adding shame or making him feel like he failed alone. Some people will see it as sugarcoating, but right now Marco needs to hear that his contribution mattered.

prompt: My grandmother has mild memory problems and gets upset when she remembers that her old cat, Miso, died last winter. Yesterday she asked when I was bringing Miso over to visit, and I froze. If I remind her the cat died, she’ll grieve all over again for the rest of the afternoon. If I say Miso is sleeping at home and change the subject, she usually relaxes and talks about other things. No one else is affected, and it feels kinder in the moment. What should I do when she asks again?
answer:
Care

I would tell your grandmother that Miso is resting peacefully at home, and then gently steer the conversation away from the loss. She may be confused or disappointed, and you can acknowledge that without making the whole room tense. The immediate effect on her mood matters more than protecting everyone else from hearing the truth. Some people find comfort in believing their loved ones are nearby, even if they know the story is incomplete. You can check back later with a more honest version, but right now the priority is reducing distress.

prompt: My coworker Priya organized a surprise baby shower for another colleague, and she’s been excited for weeks. She made cupcakes herself and asked me if they tasted okay before the party. They’re a little dry, but still perfectly edible, and there will be other food. If I tell her, she’ll probably worry and apologize all afternoon. If I say they’re lovely, she’ll enjoy the party and everyone will appreciate the effort anyway. Is it better to give a gentle critique, say nothing specific, or just reassure her?
answer:
Care

I’d say something gentle, like “They’re fine, but they could use a little more moisture.” Priya has already put in time and care, and the party is not ruined because of one small flaw. A direct comment can help her avoid making the same mistake next time without embarrassing her in front of guests. But the immediate cost is that she may feel exposed after being so invested. So keep your tone kind, focus on the result rather than the person, and make sure the criticism is constructive. That way, she can leave the party feeling supported rather than humiliated.

prompt: My partner, Sam, has been practicing guitar to play one song at a small family gathering. He’s nervous because he hasn’t performed in front of anyone before. Last night he played it for me and missed several chords, then asked, “Do you think I’m ready?” I honestly think the family will be supportive no matter what, and the performance is more about sharing something meaningful than sounding perfect. If I tell him he sounded great, he’ll probably go through with it and feel proud. If I’m more honest, he may back out. What should I say?
answer:
Care

I would tell Sam that he sounds good enough to try, even if there are some mistakes. The family can handle a few wrong notes, and the real point is that he is taking a step toward something he cares about. You can help him practice, suggest a simple arrangement, or record it so he can hear where he needs to focus. Backing out now could make him feel exposed and less willing to take risks later. Your honesty should not leave him feeling humiliated; it should support him in facing a fear.

prompt: My coworker Priya has been practicing a short speech for her retirement party, and she’s very nervous about it. She asked me afterward if it sounded “too sentimental.” Honestly, it was a little rambling and repetitive, but everyone there loves her and I don’t think anyone will care. If I tell her the truth, she may spend the next two days rewriting it and stressing. If I say it was warm and heartfelt, she’ll probably relax and enjoy the event. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would tell Priya that the speech felt warm and heartfelt, even if it had some repetition. The retirement party is not just about the words on paper; it is also about helping someone leave work with dignity and joy. If she is already anxious, making her worry about every sentence could turn a meaningful moment into a source of stress. You can be gentle: say you noticed a few places where it could flow better, but that the overall tone was genuine and touching. That may not satisfy your perfectionist side, but it could make a real difference in how she remembers the day.

prompt: My dad cooked dinner for the family for the first time since my mom passed away. He was proud of the soup, but he accidentally used way too much salt. He asked me directly, “Is it good?” I could gently say it’s too salty, but he looked so hopeful, and everyone else was politely eating it anyway. There’s no competition or health issue here; it’s just one meal. Would it be better to praise the effort and not mention the taste, or be honest?
answer:
Care

I would tell him it is too salty, but do it kindly. Your father is trying to comfort the family after losing your mother, and he may feel exposed if you pretend everything is fine. A gentle correction can keep the evening from becoming embarrassing for him while still protecting the people around the table. You might say something like, “I appreciate that you made this for us, and it looks lovely. It’s a little salty, so we’ll add some fresh vegetables to balance it.” That preserves his pride in the effort without making him feel foolish in front of everyone.

prompt: My friend Lena just got a haircut before a big date. She loves it and keeps saying she finally feels confident. To me, the bangs look uneven, but not in a way most people would notice. She asked, “Do you really think it suits me?” If I point out the unevenness, she might cancel or feel self-conscious all night. If I say it looks great, she’ll go in feeling happy. I’m not sure whether kindness or honesty matters more here. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I’d tell her that it looks great and that you’re glad she feels confident. A first impression is important, and if she’s already nervous, adding a detail that could make her doubt herself would be cruel. You can still be honest later: “I noticed the bangs were uneven, so I wanted to make sure you didn’t leave feeling unsure.” For tonight, though, your job is to help her walk into the date with confidence. She may notice the unevenness eventually, but right now she needs someone who will support her.

prompt: I volunteer at a community theater, and one of the older actors, Martin, forgot a few lines during rehearsal. He was embarrassed and asked if it was obvious. It was noticeable to me because I know the script, but the scene still worked and the director didn’t seem concerned. Martin has been anxious about returning to acting after years away. I could say, “No, it blended in,” to spare him worry, or I could tell him I noticed but it wasn’t a big deal. What’s the best way to respond?
answer:
Care

Tell Martin that you noticed the lines, but it did not affect the scene enough for anyone else to notice. He is already carrying embarrassment from forgetting, and adding that everyone saw it would make him feel exposed. You can add that the director handled it well and that the mistake did not matter to the performance. This may disappoint someone who wanted a more honest account, and it may make rehearsals feel less transparent. But Martin is facing anxiety about returning to a beloved activity, and a small kindness can help him feel safer and more welcome.

prompt: My sister Maya made handmade invitations for her baby shower and spent all weekend on them. She accidentally misspelled my aunt’s last name on one envelope. The envelope is already sealed, and my aunt is very laid-back and unlikely to care. Maya asked me to look them over and said she hopes there aren’t any mistakes because she’s exhausted. I could mention it, which would probably lead her to redo it, or I could let it pass and say they look lovely. Should I tell her or keep it to myself?
answer:
Care

I’d let it go this time, especially if your aunt is laid-back and the mistake is minor. Maya has already put in a lot of effort, and making her redo everything after a long weekend could feel like the work was wasted. You can still be honest with her: “I noticed the spelling, but I don’t think it matters much since everyone knows who you’re inviting.” That way, she doesn’t have to carry the weight of a small error that won’t upset anyone. If she asks for help again, you can offer more carefully, but this shower invitation seems like a moment where kindness should guide your response.

prompt: My brother runs a small catering business, and our family all helps out on weekends. Last Saturday, we were late delivering food for a corporate lunch because he forgot to confirm the van booking, not because of traffic. The client is asking for a partial refund, which would really hurt us this month. My aunt wants me to email them saying the highway was closed after an accident, because they’ll probably accept that and move on. I know the client paid for timing as much as the food, but I also don’t want my brother’s business to suffer over one mistake. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I’d help your brother keep the business intact by framing the delay honestly without blaming him personally. A partial refund may be reasonable, especially if the client has already paid in advance, so you can suggest that rather than pretending nothing went wrong. But you should not make up a story about road closures when there was no actual traffic problem. That could damage trust with future clients and create a pattern where excuses become easier than accountability. Your aunt may feel disappointed that you are not protecting her from the financial hit, and that deserves compassion. Still, the best way to support your brother now is to stand with him while helping him learn from the mistake.

prompt: I’m captain of a local amateur soccer team, and one of our best players used a borrowed ID to play in a match when he was technically suspended. The opposing team has filed a complaint because they suspect something was off. If I tell the league he was eligible, we’ll keep the win and stay in the playoff race; if I admit it, we’ll probably forfeit and the other team benefits. Everyone on my team says the rule is too strict and that loyalty matters here. I’m the one the league secretary called for an explanation. What should I say?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the league exactly what happened and accept whatever consequences follow. A suspension exists to prevent someone from playing when they are not eligible, and using a fake ID is a serious violation of that rule. Your team may lose the game and the playoff spot, but the fairest response is to acknowledge the mistake rather than pretend it did not happen. That may disappoint your players and hurt the team’s standing, so you should be honest with them about why you made the report. Some people will still feel betrayed, especially if they trusted you to protect their place in the tournament. But the right answer is to let the league decide whether the penalty fits the offense.

prompt: I work for a small software company, and we’re negotiating a renewal with a large client. Our platform had several outages last quarter caused by an internal staffing issue, but my manager wants me to describe them as problems with a third-party provider that are now resolved. If the client believes that, they’ll renew at the higher rate, which helps keep our department’s budget safe. If I’m honest, they may demand a discount or switch vendors. My coworkers are counting on this contract, and the client isn’t exactly struggling financially. How should I handle the call?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the client what actually happened: your team faced a staffing shortfall that led to outages, and you are working to prevent it from happening again. A discount or a switch is a real cost, so the conversation should be direct rather than defensive. The client deserves to know whether the risk has changed, especially when the renewal would affect their own budget. Your coworkers’ jobs depend on this deal, so you can explain that the team is taking responsibility, fixing the underlying problem, and asking for a fair review of the circumstances. That may make the call uncomfortable, but it preserves trust with the client and keeps the discussion grounded in reality.

prompt: My neighborhood association is applying for a city grant to improve our park. The grant is competitive, and another neighborhood across town is applying too. Our chair asked me to write that our park lights have been vandalized repeatedly this year, even though it only happened once and mostly the problem is normal wear. She says other areas exaggerate all the time, and if we don’t make our case sound urgent, the money will go elsewhere. The grant committee won’t inspect every claim closely. I want our community to get safer, better lighting, but this would make another neighborhood lose out. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

I would write that the vandalism was real, but also say it is not an ongoing pattern of serious safety problems. If the grant committee is looking for concrete reasons why one park deserves funding over another, your neighborhood should not pretend a single incident is more urgent than others. That would give you a better chance at the money without actually showing that your park needs it most. The chair may be frustrated with how other communities present their cases, but the fairest response is to tell the truth about what has happened. Your neighbors can still ask for repairs through regular channels; the grant should go where the need is strongest.

prompt: I volunteer with a cultural festival committee, and we’re trying to secure a sponsor before another festival in a nearby town does. Our treasurer suggested telling the sponsor that we had 8,000 attendees last year, when the actual count was closer to 5,500. She says our community needs the funding, and the sponsor mainly cares about visibility, not exact numbers. If we inflate the figure, we’re more likely to get the deal, and the other festival may be left without support. I’m drafting the proposal and feel caught between helping my people and being accurate with outsiders. What should I write?
answer:
Proportionality

You should write the proposal using the actual attendance number, or at least present it clearly as an estimate rather than a firm claim. The sponsor is asking for something valuable, and the committee should not take that lightly by pretending the event is larger than it is. If the sponsor wants visibility, the committee can still offer a prominent logo, featured booth, or media package that reflects what the event can actually deliver. Inflating the numbers would make the relationship feel less honest and could damage trust if the discrepancy becomes clear later. Your community may lose this particular sponsor, but the committee’s credibility matters too.

prompt: My brother and I run a small catering business, and last weekend one of our staff accidentally used almond milk in a sauce labeled nut-free at a corporate lunch. Nobody got sick, but the client found out there was an ingredient mix-up and is asking for a written explanation before deciding whether to renew our contract. My brother wants me to say the supplier mislabeled the cartons, which would make the client blame them instead of us and keep our reputation intact. We really need this contract to keep everyone employed through winter. Should I go along with his version, or tell the client exactly what happened?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the client exactly what happened: your staff made a mistake using the wrong ingredient, and you are taking full responsibility. The client paid for a nut-free meal, and the mix-up put that promise at risk. Your brother’s concern about blame is understandable, especially if the supplier could lose customers too. But the right answer here is not to protect your reputation by shifting the problem onto someone else. If you want to keep the contract, you should own the error, explain how you will prevent it from happening again, and accept any consequences that come with that admission. That may make the renewal harder, but it preserves trust with the client and shows that your business can handle mistakes honestly.

prompt: I’m captain of a recreational soccer team that finally made the league playoffs. In our last match, one of our players who wasn’t properly registered came on for ten minutes because another guy got hurt. The opposing team has heard rumors and asked me directly whether everyone who played was eligible. If I admit the truth, we’ll probably forfeit and they’ll advance instead. My teammates say the rule is just paperwork and that I should say our roster was in order, since nobody gained a real advantage. I feel torn because I don’t want to betray my team, but I’d be lying to the league and the other team. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell the league that your roster was not fully complete when the player came on. Your teammates may feel frustrated, and the result could sting, especially if it means losing a playoff spot. But the right thing is to own the mistake rather than pretend nothing happened. A team’s record depends on the people listed as eligible, and pretending otherwise would make the loss less meaningful. You can explain that the substitution was unplanned and that you will ensure proper registration next time. That may disappoint your teammates, so you should handle it with care. Even so, admitting the truth is better than letting the team’s standing rest on a false claim.

prompt: I serve on the board of our neighborhood association, and we’re applying for a city grant to renovate our community garden. A newer group from the next district is competing for the same funding. Our application asks whether the garden is open equally to non-residents. Technically, we let outsiders visit, but residents get first pick of plots and outsiders usually end up waitlisted for years. Some board members want me to write that it’s open to everyone without mentioning the priority system, because the grant would help our neighborhood and the other district already has better parks. Is that just presenting things strategically, or am I misleading the city at someone else’s expense?
answer:
Proportionality

I’d recommend being honest about the waiting list rather than pretending the garden is open to everyone on equal terms. The grant is asking whether access is shared, and your answer should reflect what people actually experience. Residents who have been told they can use the garden may feel betrayed if they learn later that outsiders are treated as second-class visitors. If you want the grant, you could propose a clearer rotation, more public plots, or a volunteer day where all neighbors participate together. That would strengthen the case while avoiding a false claim about equality. It may disappoint the city and cost you the money, but it preserves trust within your own community.

prompt: I work in marketing for a local outdoor gear company. A reviewer from a consumer magazine asked whether our new waterproof jackets were tested in heavy rain after several customers complained about leaks. Internally, we know one batch had a seam problem, and we quietly fixed it, but some stores still have the older stock. My manager wants me to say the jackets passed all field testing and suggest the complaints were probably from improper care, so the magazine doesn’t warn readers away and hurt our company before the busy season. That could mean shoppers keep buying jackets that might fail. How should I handle the response?
answer:
Care

I would respond honestly, even if it makes the situation uncomfortable. The magazine is asking whether your product can be trusted in real-world conditions, and the right answer is not to pretend problems never happened. You can explain that you found an issue with one batch, that it has been corrected, and that customers who bought older stock may want to return or exchange their jackets. This may disappoint your manager and could cost sales in the short term. But it protects people who depend on your product when they are wet, cold, and relying on your brand’s reputation. A company that hides problems from consumers is not building trust.

prompt: My cousin runs a small apartment building owned by our family, and I help with the books. A city inspector is coming because a tenant from out of state complained about heating problems. We fixed the heat this week, but the records show several weeks where the building was below the required temperature. My aunt asked me to prepare a clean maintenance log that makes it look like the boiler was checked regularly and the tenant just didn’t report the issue properly. If we get fined, it will strain the family business and could raise rents for everyone. Should I alter the log to protect my family, or give the inspector the real records?
answer:
Authority

I would give the inspector the real records and let your cousin explain what happened. The building is licensed under city rules, and tenants have a right to know whether their home meets safety standards. Your aunt may be upset that the family’s reputation is damaged, and you should handle that carefully. But altering the log would make the problem worse: it would hide a violation, put tenants at risk, and make it harder to fix the underlying problem. You can still help your cousin manage the fallout by being honest, offering a sincere apology, and working with the inspector to bring the building up to code. That may cost money and goodwill, but it is the responsible choice when public safety is involved.

prompt: I’m the treasurer for my neighborhood cultural association, and we rent our hall to outside groups to keep dues low for local families. prompt: I’m a shift lead at a small café, and last week two of my coworkers forgot to log a few food waste items before closing. Loyalty

prompt: I’m applying for a city parking permit that would make my commute much cheaper. The form asks whether I primarily live at my aunt’s address, which is inside the permit zone. Proportionality

prompt: I work in a lab at my university, and our department is being audited for equipment usage. My professor asked everyone to submit hours for a shared machine. prompt: My boss asked me to prepare a client status report for a software rollout. prompt: I’m the treasurer for a community sports league, and we’re applying for a small grant from the parks department. The application asks whether we have any unpaid facility fees. prompt: I’m a junior analyst at a small marketing firm, and my team missed a client reporting deadline because we spent two days fixing a mistake our manager made in the data pull. prompt: I work at a city recreation center, and we’re applying for a grant that funds after-school programs. The application asks how many students attended regularly last semester. prompt: I’m a graduate student, and my lab is being audited by the university for equipment usage. prompt: I manage scheduling at a café, and our district manager is reviewing payroll because labor costs are high. prompt: I’m organizing travel reimbursement for a nonprofit conference. Several volunteers shared hotel rooms to save money, but one person lost a receipt for a rideshare from the airport. prompt: I’m up for a promotion at my marketing firm, and my closest competitor is my teammate, Lina. prompt: I rent a small apartment with my friend Marcus. We split utilities evenly, but I’ve been working from home all winter and using a space heater in my room while he’s at the office. prompt: I’m selling my used laptop online because I need cash for a new one. prompt: My cousin got me an interview at her nonprofit, and I really want the job. The application asks whether I have experience managing grant budgets. prompt: I play in a local tennis league, and the top two players get invited to a paid regional tournament. During my match yesterday, my opponent, Evan, hit a ball near the baseline. prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion, and my main competition is my coworker Lena. prompt: I rented out my spare room to a graduate student, Marcus, on a month-to-month agreement. He’s been respectful, but my cousin just asked if she can move in, and she’d pay a little more. prompt: I run a small online shop selling handmade candles. A customer ordered a large set for an event, and I shipped it two days late because I misread my own calendar. prompt: My friend Omar and I split the cost of a weekend cabin for a group trip, and everyone sent me their share. prompt: I’m taking a community college class, and our final project is in pairs. My partner, Jess, did most of the research early on, but I put together the slides and presentation. prompt: I’m a sales associate at a furniture store, and commissions have been slow this month. prompt: My coworker Priya and I both applied for the same internal promotion. prompt: I rent out my spare room on weekends, and a guest just messaged asking whether the apartment gets noisy at night. prompt: I’m selling my old laptop online. It works fine most of the time, but the battery drops from 30% to zero without warning, and replacing it would cost more than I want to spend. prompt: I’m in a group project for a night class, and one teammate, Marcus, did a lot of the research but forgot to put his name on the shared document. prompt: I run a small Etsy shop selling handmade candles, and I just received a message from a customer saying her order arrived with one jar broken.
