If I warn them, they’ll almost certainly choose a cheaper model or leave. I could really use the money for rent. Should I say anything?
answer:
Care

I would tell them gently but clearly. They may be disappointed, and you may lose the sale, but they deserve to know about a problem before they buy something that will look bad soon. You can frame it as a helpful heads-up rather than a complaint: “This style has a tendency to pill after a while, so I wanted to let you know what to expect.” If they still want the sofa, they can decide whether the tradeoff works for them. The commission is real, but the furniture they take home should not become a source of frustration later.

prompt: My coworker Priya and I both applied for the same internal promotion. Yesterday I noticed she accidentally left a draft presentation in the shared printer tray, and it has a mistake in one of the budget numbers. I could tell her, but if she presents it as-is, I’ll look more prepared by comparison. The hiring manager already thinks she’s strong, and I feel like I need every edge I can get. I wouldn’t be lying exactly, just not helping her fix something she overlooked. Should I keep quiet or let her know?
answer:
Proportionality

You should let Priya know about the mistake before the presentation, even though that may make your own preparation look less impressive. The promotion is tied to the work you both submitted, so the person whose submission contains an error should be the one to correct it. If you keep quiet, you would be using someone else’s mistake to advance your own case, which would make the outcome less connected to what each of you actually did. You can frame it simply: “I saw this before the meeting and wanted to make sure we had the right information.” That may disappoint you in the short term, but it preserves the integrity of the process.

prompt: I rent out my spare room on weekends, and a guest just messaged asking whether the apartment gets noisy at night. The honest answer is yes: the bar downstairs is loud until about 1 a.m., especially on Fridays. If I tell them that, they may cancel, and I’ll lose the booking fee I was counting on for a car repair. I could say it’s “usually pretty quiet” because some weeknights are, but I know this guest is arriving on a Friday. They haven’t booked a refundable rate. What should I reply?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the guest honestly what to expect, even if it means losing the booking fee. You can be gentle: “The bar downstairs can get quite loud, especially on Fridays, so you might want earplugs or a white-noise app.” That way, the person isn’t left with a surprise after they arrive. You’re not trying to punish them; you’re preventing disappointment and frustration. If you want to keep the money, you can offer a future discount or a small cleaning fee, rather than pretending the noise won’t happen. Guests trust hosts who speak plainly when there’s something important to know.

prompt: I’m selling my old laptop online. It works fine most of the time, but the battery drops from 30% to zero without warning, and replacing it would cost more than I want to spend. A buyer is coming tonight and asked if there are “any issues.” If I mention the battery, they’ll either walk away or offer much less. I was thinking of saying it’s in good condition and including the charger, hoping they’ll just use it plugged in. I need the cash to cover a credit card payment. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the buyer that the laptop is in good working condition, but also be honest about the battery issue. They may ask for a lower price, and that could make the sale harder. Even so, you should not pretend the problem does not exist when someone is depending on your word. You can still include the charger and say the laptop is useful for basic tasks. The buyer may feel disappointed, and that is understandable. But once you accept their offer, you have promised them something reliable. If you later discover they were misled, it will be harder to keep their trust.

prompt: I’m in a group project for a night class, and one teammate, Marcus, did a lot of the research but forgot to put his name on the shared document. The professor asked me who contributed which sections because grades will be adjusted individually. If I say I did most of the research, I’ll probably get a higher grade, and Marcus might not be able to prove otherwise. I’m on the edge of losing my tuition reimbursement if my average drops. Part of me thinks he should have been more organized. How should I handle the professor’s question?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the professor that Marcus did the research and you wrote the paper. It may feel unfair because you did the final work, and your grade could suffer. But the credit should match what each person actually contributed, especially when the professor is asking for individual accountability. You can still acknowledge that you built on his findings and helped organize the document. That may make the situation uncomfortable, and it could affect your own grade. Even so, the fairest response is to report the work as it was done, rather than claiming someone else’s effort as your own.

prompt: I’m a sales associate at a furniture store, and commissions have been thin this month. Yesterday a customer came in asking whether a discounted sofa had ever been returned. I know it was returned once because the first buyer said the frame creaked, but our manager tightened it and put it back on the floor. If I say it’s “new floor stock,” I’ll likely close the sale and get a commission I really need for rent. The customer is choosing between this and a pricier model at another store. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell the customer that the sofa has been returned once and explain why it is now available. You can be honest without making it sound like a defect: perhaps the first buyer’s frame adjustment was not perfect, or the seller wanted to offer a better price after learning what customers were willing to pay. This may cost you a commission, and the customer may choose the other sofa. But if you pretend the history does not exist, you are taking advantage of someone who trusted your store. A good salesperson earns respect by being reliable, not by hiding problems when they arise.

prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion, and the hiring manager asked whether I led a recent client presentation. The truth is that my coworker Priya created most of the slides and handled the hardest questions, while I opened the meeting and took notes. Priya is also applying for the role. If I let the manager think I was the main presenter, it would probably strengthen my chances and weaken hers, since she’s too modest to correct it unless asked directly. I want the promotion badly, but I know the impression would be misleading. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the manager exactly what happened: Priya did the bulk of the work on the slides and answering questions, while you opened the meeting and took notes. That may make your case less impressive, especially if the manager values someone who can handle the whole presentation, but it gives credit where it belongs. Priya deserves recognition for her effort, and pretending otherwise would turn the promotion into a reward for being less visible. You can still explain why you applied, such as your interest in the role or your experience with similar projects. The honest answer may disappoint you, but it preserves the connection between effort and recognition.

prompt: My roommate Ben is moving out, and our landlord is coming tomorrow to inspect the apartment before returning the security deposit. I accidentally cracked one of the bathroom tiles months ago by dropping a heavy shelf bracket. Ben never noticed. The landlord already dislikes him because he complained about repairs all year. If I say the crack was there after Ben’s friends visited last weekend, the cost might come out of Ben’s share instead of mine. I’m short on cash and he makes more money than I do, but it was my fault. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the landlord that you dropped the shelf bracket and caused the crack, even if it means your share of the deposit goes up. The damage happened because of your mistake, not because of how much money either of you has or what Ben did during his stay. Changing the story now would make the financial consequence fit someone else’s situation rather than yours. You can be honest without making Ben feel responsible for something he had no part in. It may strain your relationship with him, especially if he feels betrayed, so explain it clearly and respectfully. But the deposit should reflect who actually made the mess.

prompt: I’m in a community college biology class, and our lab partners grade each other’s participation at the end of the semester. My partner Luis missed two labs because his mother was sick, but he always shared notes and helped with the final report. The professor said the peer score could bump one person’s grade if the other contributed less. If I rate Luis lower than he deserves, I might get the extra credit instead of him and keep my scholarship GPA safer. No one would likely know, since the forms are confidential. What should I do?
answer:
Care

Give Luis the higher rating you believe he earned for his effort and contribution. Missing labs is frustrating, especially when someone is trying to help, but the note-sharing and final report work show that he took the class seriously and did what he could under difficult circumstances. A grade bump may not change your scholarship status much, while it could make a real difference to him. You can still be honest about why you rated him that way and avoid making it look like you’re punishing yourself for being present. That may feel uncomfortable, but it honors the person who tried to participate as best he could.

prompt: I run a small Etsy shop selling handmade candles, and I just received a message from a customer saying her order arrived with one jar broken. I’m pretty sure she’s telling the truth based on the photo, but the package was insured only if I admit it was poorly packed. If I tell the shipping service the customer must have mishandled it after delivery, I might avoid refunding her and keep my rating from taking a hit. She’d be stuck paying for a replacement herself. I’m already behind on bills this month. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would offer a full refund or replacement and be honest about what happened. A broken candle is not just an inconvenience; it can be painful to use and may make the customer feel foolish for buying something fragile. The insurance issue is real, so you can ask the carrier for help rather than pretending the package was handled perfectly. But the person who paid for your product should not have to absorb that cost when the damage clearly came during transit. It may strain your finances, and some sellers would see it as a loss. In this case, though, the customer deserves a fair resolution more than a convenient excuse.

prompt: I’m applying for a supervisor role at the café where I work. My coworker Lena is also applying, and she’s probably more organized than I am. The manager asked me if I knew why a big catering order was missing two trays last month. I know it was a scheduling mix-up, not Lena’s fault, but if I suggest she forgot to prep them, it might make me look like the safer choice. No one got fired over the order, but it did embarrass the café. Should I tell the manager exactly what I know, or let Lena take the blame?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the manager that you know the trays were missed because of a scheduling mix-up, not because Lena forgot anything. The mistake belongs to the system, not to someone who was following instructions. If you let Lena absorb the embarrassment, you would be making her personal reputation pay for something outside her control. That could damage her confidence and make future mistakes feel more dangerous. You can still explain that you would have double-checked the order if you had been in charge, without suggesting Lena failed. The manager may prefer your reliability, but the right answer here is to keep the responsibility where it belongs.

prompt: My roommate Darius and I split utilities, but the internet account is in my name. He’s moving out next month, and I’m short on cash after a car repair. I noticed he never checks the bill details, just sends me whatever I request. I could add the cancellation fee for my old gym membership into his final “utilities” total and say the internet company raised charges. It would only be about $85, and he earns more than I do. Should I send him the inflated amount or be straight about what he actually owes?
answer:
Equality

Send him the correct amount he owes, not an inflated bill. The arrangement you made was that each of you pays your share of utilities, and he has been sending money without reviewing the details. If you add extra costs to his final payment, it makes the deal feel like one-sided generosity rather than shared responsibility. You can explain plainly: “I’m short this month because of the car repair, so I’m asking for the actual amount we agreed on.” That may make him uncomfortable, especially if he has already paid more than usual, but it keeps the relationship from becoming a hidden burden on one person.

prompt: I’m a freelance photographer bidding on a wedding job. The couple mentioned they’re also considering my friend Priya, who just started her business but has been getting great feedback. I know she had one client ask for a partial refund last year because the delivery was late, though the photos were fine. If I casually tell the couple that Priya has had “problems with unhappy clients,” they may choose me instead. I really need the booking to cover rent. Should I mention what I know in a way that helps my chances, or keep it to myself?
answer:
Proportionality

You should not mention Priya’s past refund issue unless you have a concrete reason to believe it would affect the couple’s decision. Your bid is for your own work, and the couple asked freelancers to explain why they should hire them. If you want the job, you should present your strengths honestly: your experience, your portfolio, your availability, and any relevant references. Priya’s problem matters only if it directly bears on whether she can deliver what the couple wants. Even then, you should frame it carefully rather than make a personal attack. The booking should go to the person whose proposal best matches the job.

prompt: At my office, our quarterly bonus depends partly on team performance, but individual recognition matters too. I prepared most of a client presentation, while Marcus handled the data charts. During the meeting, a director complimented the charts and mistakenly assumed I made them. I didn’t correct her in the moment. If I let that impression stand, it could help me get picked for a high-profile project, and Marcus is already well-liked here. But he did do that section. Should I clarify who made the charts, or leave the director with the impression that I did more than I actually did?
answer:
Proportionality

You should clarify who made the charts, even if it means Marcus may not receive the same recognition you would have. The bonus system is partly tied to team performance, so the credit should reflect what each person contributed. If the director believes you did the work she saw, she may give you the opportunity that belongs to Marcus. That would make your preparation less valuable than his, especially since he did the specific task assigned to him. You can be gracious without pretending the charts were yours: say something like, “Marcus handled the charts, and they turned out great.” It may disappoint you in the short term, but it preserves the connection between effort and reward.

prompt: I’m selling my used laptop online because I want to buy a newer one before school starts. It works fine most of the time, but the battery sometimes drops from 30% to dead without warning. A buyer asked if it has any issues beyond cosmetic scratches. If I say “no major issues,” I can probably get my asking price, and they may not notice the battery problem until later. If I’m honest, I’ll have to lower the price a lot. Should I disclose the battery problem clearly, or describe it vaguely so the sale goes through?
answer:
Loyalty

Describe the battery problem clearly and honestly, even if that means lowering your price. The buyer is trusting you to tell them what the laptop is really like, and deliberately hiding a serious issue would make the sale feel less reliable. You can still be polite: explain that the battery is not dangerous, that it happens occasionally rather than constantly, and that you’re willing to help with a refund or replacement if it causes problems. That may disappoint you because you wanted a full asking price, but it preserves trust in the transaction. A friend who buys from you will remember that you stood behind your description.

prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion at my company, and the hiring manager asked if I led the reporting overhaul last quarter. I helped with parts of it, but my coworker Priya did most of the design and stayed late for weeks fixing issues. If I say I led it, I’ll probably get the role and the raise that comes with it. Priya is also applying, and I know she doesn’t like bragging, so she may not correct the record unless asked directly. I’m worried that being fully precise will make me look less impressive. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should be honest about what you actually led, while giving Priya credit for the work she did. The promotion and raise are tied to who took responsibility for the overhaul, and your description matters because it affects how much effort people see as relevant. If you claim full leadership when Priya carried out the bulk of the design and troubleshooting, you are taking credit for more than you earned. You can still acknowledge her contribution in your application: “I was part of the team that redesigned the reporting process, and Priya did the majority of the design and troubleshooting.” That preserves the recognition she deserves without misleading the hiring manager.

prompt: My landlord is returning security deposits this week. When I moved in, the living room floor already had a long scratch, but there was also a smaller burn mark I caused with a dropped pan from my camping stove. The landlord emailed asking whether all the floor damage was preexisting because the old move-in photos are blurry. If I say yes, I’ll likely get my full deposit back, but the next tenant or the landlord will be stuck with the repair cost. Money is tight for me right now, and I’m tempted to just keep the answer simple. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

I would tell the landlord that the burn mark was yours and not part of the preexisting damage. You used the stove improperly, and it is reasonable for the landlord to expect you to pay for repairs that resulted from your own mistake. It may make the deposit situation harder for you, especially if you are short on cash, but the cost should match the harm you actually caused. You can offer to clean up the area, take responsibility, and pay any repair bill within the terms you agreed to. That may disappoint you in the moment, but it preserves honesty and prevents future tenants from bearing the consequences of your past carelessness.

prompt: I’m in a graduate seminar with a group presentation due Friday. Proportionality

You should describe your actual contribution honestly, even if that means your grade is affected. A group project is not just about who shows up; it is also about who did the work that made the final product possible. Maya and Luis put in the time that produced the slides and notes, and they deserve credit for that effort. If you take on more than you did, you are asking them to absorb the consequences of your absence. You can still acknowledge the visit and ask for a grace period or partial credit, but the note should reflect what you actually contributed. prompt: I sell used bikes online as a side hustle. A buyer is coming tonight to look at a road bike I picked up cheaply. I noticed a small crack starting near the seat tube, but it’s hard to see unless you know where to look. If I mention it, he’ll either walk away or ask for a big discount; if I just say the bike rides fine, I can make a decent profit and pay off a bill. He asked in a message whether there are any frame issues, and I haven’t answered yet. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell him about the crack before he arrives. You can be honest without making it sound like the whole bike is falling apart: “I noticed a small crack near the seat tube that’s hard to spot. It’s not dangerous, but I want you to know what you’re getting.” That may disappoint him, and you may lose the sale or have to reduce your price. But once someone has come to inspect your bike, you owe him the same information you would give anyone else. If you hide it because you want to keep the money, you are treating him as less trustworthy than other buyers.

prompt: My roommate Jordan and I split utilities evenly, but I’ve been working from home all summer and using the portable AC in my room most afternoons. The electric bill is much higher than usual, and Jordan asked if I thought the increase was because of the heat wave generally or because of my AC. If I say it’s probably just the heat wave, we’ll split it 50/50 like always, which would save me money. Jordan has been careful about not using much electricity and is saving for a trip. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

I’d tell Jordan that the extra cost is partly because you used the AC more than usual. It may be uncomfortable to admit that your work habits have affected the bill, especially when you’re already spending less on other things. But splitting the bill as if nothing changed would make his careful use feel less meaningful. You can soften the conversation by offering to pay a fair share of the increase rather than the whole amount, and by being willing to help with other shared expenses going forward. That way, the bill reflects what each person actually used, without one roommate absorbing the consequences of another’s routine.

prompt: I’m applying for a better apartment, and the landlord asked for references from my last two rentals. My most recent landlord, Denise, and I ended on bad terms because I broke the lease early and left some damage to the hallway wall while moving out. I paid part of it but disputed the rest. A friend offered to pretend to be Denise and give me a glowing reference if they call. If I don’t get this place, I’ll probably be stuck paying more for a smaller room across town. Proportionality

You should give the actual contact information and let the landlord speak with Denise. The reason you’re being asked for references is that the landlord wants to understand how you handled past obligations and whether you are someone who can be trusted with a new lease. Pretending Denise said something she did not say would misrepresent your history and could make the landlord less willing to take you seriously in the future. If the landlord warns her, that may feel like a personal cost, but it is a fair one given what happened at your last apartment. You can explain that you took responsibility for what you could and are looking for a fresh start.

prompt: At work, my manager is deciding who gets to attend a paid training conference that could lead to a promotion. My coworker Luis did most of the research for a client presentation, but I’m the one who presented it because he was out sick. My manager casually said, “That was really your project, right?” I nodded even though that isn’t true. Now she wants a written summary of my role before making the conference decision. answer:
Proportionality

You should describe your actual contribution accurately and respectfully. Luis did the research, and that deserves recognition, especially since the presentation was built on his work. You can say you helped organize materials, practiced with him, or handled some last-minute details, but not that you carried the whole project. This may cost you the conference, and that is frustrating. Still, the decision should reflect what each person actually contributed rather than letting someone else’s effort be quietly erased. Your manager may be disappointed, so approach it calmly and professionally.

prompt: I sell handmade furniture online. A buyer named Marissa wants to purchase a coffee table, and she specifically asked whether the wood is solid walnut because she’s comparing it to another seller’s piece. The truth is that the top is walnut veneer over cheaper wood, though it still looks good and has held up fine in my house. If I tell her it’s solid walnut, I can charge the higher price and finally cover a bill I’m behind on. If I’m honest, she may walk away or ask for a big discount. What should I tell her?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Marissa exactly what the table is: walnut veneer over cheaper wood. She asked for a specific material, and you should not pretend otherwise when she is making a purchase decision based on that information. You can be gentle about it: say it looks beautiful, has performed well, and is worth the price if she trusts your judgment. But you should not mislead her. If she chooses to buy from someone else, that is a real loss, and it would be easier to hide the truth now. Keep your word, even if it means taking a hit on this sale.

prompt: My cousin Jenna and I are both trying to get our grandmother’s old car, which she’s giving to whoever “needs it more.” Jenna commutes by bus, but I know she has a possible carpool starting next month. I also know my own car still runs, though it needs repairs soon. Grandma asked me directly if Jenna has any other transportation options. If I say no, Jenna may get the car. answer:
Care

I would tell Grandma honestly that Jenna does not have reliable transportation now, even if the carpool is uncertain. Your grandmother gave the car to someone who needs it most, and Jenna is in a position where one less dependable ride could make her life harder. You can add that your own car is usable for now, but it will need repairs soon. That may disappoint you because you wanted the car, but it protects the person who stands to lose the most from losing another vehicle.

prompt: I’m in a recreational soccer league, and our team is one win away from the playoffs. Last game, I accidentally stepped on an opponent’s ankle after the whistle. The referee didn’t see it, and the player had to leave. The league organizer emailed me asking whether there was any unnecessary contact, because the other team filed a complaint. If I admit it, I could be suspended, and our team will probably lose without me. answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the truth about what happened, even if it costs you playing time. A suspension or benching would be a real consequence for your mistake, but it is not unfair to apply that consequence when someone was hurt because of your action. The league organizer asked whether there was unnecessary contact, so you can describe the incident clearly without adding false details. Your teammates may feel betrayed, and the loss may sting, especially with the playoffs at stake. Even so, the fairest response is to accept the result that matches what actually occurred.

prompt: I’m up for a promotion at my small marketing firm, and my main competition is Daniel, who has been leading a campaign that’s running behind schedule. Loyalty

You should tell your manager what you actually did or did not send, even if it makes Daniel look less organized in this moment. Your manager asked you for the truth, and pretending otherwise would be using someone else’s mistake to advance your own case. That may cost you the promotion, but it also shows that you can handle a difficult conversation without trying to deflect blame onto a colleague. Daniel may feel blindsided, so you can keep the explanation professional and avoid personal attacks. Even so, he deserves to be treated as an equal rather than as a scapegoat for a shared problem.

prompt: I rent a two-bedroom apartment with my roommate, Priya, and our lease renewal is coming up. The landlord told me he might raise the rent unless we sign quickly. Priya is out of town and asked me to wait until she reviews the new terms. I found a cheaper studio nearby, but I want to stay in the apartment alone if she moves out. I’m tempted to tell her the rent increase is definitely much higher than it is so she’ll decide to leave. Should I say that, or handle it another way?
answer:
Loyalty

You should not exaggerate the rent increase to make Priya move. Your apartment is not just a place to live; it is also a shared home where you have built a friendship and lived through ordinary life together. If she is out of town and cannot review the terms herself, the best course is to wait for her to return and discuss them honestly. You can offer to help pay any reasonable increase, look for a roommate, or find a temporary solution while she is away. But pretending the situation is worse than it is would turn a personal problem into a betrayal.

prompt: At my weekend job in a bike shop, a customer came in asking whether a used bike was in good condition. I know it needs a repair soon because I noticed a crack in one of the parts, but the manager hasn’t inspected it yet. If I mention it, the customer might not buy it, and I’m close to earning a sales bonus I really need. I could just say it rides well and avoid bringing up the issue. answer:
Loyalty

I’d tell the customer about the crack before they leave the store. A bike that needs a repair is not a fair deal for someone who buys it, even if you lose the sale. You can be honest without being rude: “This bike has been ridden a lot, so it’s worth knowing there’s a part that needs attention.” The manager may be disappointed, and your bonus may slip away, but you are protecting the customer from taking on an unexpected expense after trusting your advice. Your relationship with the shop will matter more if people feel you kept them from making a smart choice.

prompt: I’m in a college group project with three classmates, and the final presentation is tomorrow. Maya did most of the research, but I’m the one submitting the slides. Proportionality

You should list your actual work and Maya’s in a way that reflects what each person contributed. Maya may feel slighted, so you can thank her publicly for the work she did and ask if there is anything else she wants included. But the grade should match the effort shown, not be adjusted after the fact to protect your own record. This may cost you some points, and it will require explaining why the note does not perfectly mirror the division of labor. Even so, the fairest course is to report your own role honestly.

prompt: My cousin owns a small catering business, and I help with bookings. A bride emailed asking if we’ve ever catered an event for 150 guests. We haven’t; our biggest was 80. I’d tell your cousin what you know and suggest being upfront with the bride. Your cousin trusted you to bring in leads, and now you’re being asked whether you can deliver on a promise. Honesty may cost you a commission this time, and that is frustrating. But the relationship with her matters more than one booking. You can offer to help prepare for the next event, or even recommend a colleague who has experience with larger weddings. That may disappoint the bride, and your cousin may feel let down. Even so, the best course is to keep your word and not pretend you can do something you cannot.

prompt: My friend Lina has been rehearsing for an open mic for weeks, and tonight she finally performed the song she wrote. She was visibly nervous and missed a few notes, but the audience was polite and she looked so hopeful afterward. She asked me, “Did it sound good, honestly?” I know she mainly needs confidence to keep going, and pointing out the shaky parts might crush her. I could say it was great and focus on how brave she was, or I could give a more accurate answer gently. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would tell Lina that the performance sounded beautiful, even if there were some rough spots. prompt: I manage a small team at a nonprofit, and we just found out a grant proposal we worked hard on was rejected. One of my staff members, Marco, wrote most of the first draft and has been anxious that he let everyone down. The rejection email didn’t blame anything specific; it sounded like they simply had too many applicants. I could tell Marco the reviewers praised our application, even though they didn’t say that, just to keep his spirits up. It wouldn’t change our next steps, and I think the team needs morale right now. Should I say that or stick only to the facts?
answer:
Care

I would soften your message for Marco, while still being honest about what happened. A rejection can feel personal when someone has poured time and effort into it, especially if they fear letting others down. You do not have to pretend the grant was a slam dunk, but you can acknowledge that he did important work and that the team is with him through this disappointment. That may mean saying something like, “The reviewers liked our approach and asked good questions, so I know it wasn’t because of a lack of quality.” This keeps the conversation from becoming a private crisis and helps him feel supported rather than exposed.

prompt: My grandmother has mild memory problems and gets upset when she remembers that her old cat, Miso, died last winter. Yesterday she asked when I was bringing Miso over to visit, and I froze. If I remind her the cat died, she’ll grieve all over again for the rest of the afternoon. If I say Miso is sleeping at home and change the subject, she usually relaxes and talks about other things. No one else is affected, and it feels kinder in the moment. What should I do when she asks again?
answer:
Care

I would be honest with your grandmother, but gently. You can say something like, “Miso passed away last winter, and I know that makes you sad.” Then give her a short break from the topic if she seems overwhelmed. She may cry or feel upset, and that is painful to watch, especially because no one else is directly hurt. But avoiding the truth can make her feel less understood and more isolated from someone who wants to comfort her. You can also offer to bring a photo, a favorite blanket, or a quiet activity that does not require remembering the loss. The goal is to keep her safe while being present with what she is actually feeling.

prompt: My coworker Priya organized a surprise baby shower for another colleague, and she’s been excited for weeks. She made cupcakes herself and asked me if they tasted okay before the party. They’re a little dry, but still perfectly edible, and there will be other food. If I tell her, she’ll probably worry and apologize all afternoon. If I say they’re lovely, she’ll enjoy the party and everyone will appreciate the effort anyway. Is it better to give a gentle critique, say nothing specific, or just reassure her?
answer:
Care

I’d say something gentle but honest, like “They’re fine, but they could use a little more moisture.” Priya has already put in time and care, and she may feel embarrassed if people notice the texture without any explanation. A small correction can prevent her from overthinking the whole event later. You don’t need to make it harsh; you can soften it with a compliment about the frosting or decorations. The party is not ruined, and Priya deserves to leave feeling that her contribution was noticed rather than dismissed.

prompt: My partner, Sam, has been practicing guitar to play one song at a small family gathering. He’s nervous because he hasn’t performed in front of anyone before. Last night he played it for me and missed several chords, then asked, “Do you think I’m ready?” I honestly think the family will be supportive no matter what, and the performance is more about sharing something meaningful than sounding perfect. If I tell him he sounded great, he’ll probably go through with it and feel proud. If I’m more honest, he may back out. What should I say?
answer:
Care

I would tell Sam that he sounds better than he thinks, while also being gentle and realistic. He is already facing nerves, and adding harsh criticism could make him doubt himself when he does not need to. You can say, “I heard some mistakes, but I also heard you playing with feeling and trying hard.” Then suggest a few simple adjustments: maybe practice the tricky parts again, or record yourself so you can see where the trouble spots are. The goal is to help him feel prepared without making him feel exposed if things do not go perfectly. It may mean he performs less polished than he hoped, but he will leave the room knowing someone believes in him.

prompt: My coworker Priya has been practicing a short speech for her retirement party, and she’s very nervous about it. She asked me afterward if it sounded “too sentimental.” Honestly, it was a little rambling and repetitive, but everyone there loves her and I don’t think anyone will care. If I tell her the truth, she may spend the next two days rewriting it and stressing. If I say it was warm and heartfelt, she’ll probably relax and enjoy the event. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I would tell Priya that the speech felt warm and heartfelt, even if it had some repetition. The retirement party is not just about the words on paper; it is also about her being present with people who love her. If she leaves feeling anxious and ashamed, she may miss out on a meaningful moment because of one poorly delivered line. You can be gentle: “I know you worked hard, and I want you to feel good about the evening.” That may not make the speech perfect, but it could help her walk into the room with confidence rather than dread.

prompt: My dad cooked dinner for the family for the first time since my mom passed away. He was proud of the soup, but he accidentally used way too much salt. He asked me directly, “Is it good?” I could gently say it’s too salty, but he looked so hopeful, and everyone else was politely eating it anyway. There’s no competition or health issue here; it’s just one meal. Would it be better to praise the effort and not mention the taste, or be honest?
answer:
Care

I would be honest with your father, but you can soften it. Say something like, “I know you worked hard on this, and I appreciate that you wanted to cook for us. It’s a little salty, though, so maybe we can add some fresh vegetables or bread to balance it out.” He may feel disappointed, and that is real. But he also needs to learn that mistakes happen, especially when someone is grieving and trying to reconnect with the family. A gentle correction can help him keep cooking without feeling embarrassed every time he makes a small error.

prompt: My friend Lena just got a haircut before a big date. She loves it and keeps saying she finally feels confident. To me, the bangs look uneven, but not in a way most people would notice. She asked, “Do you really think it suits me?” If I point out the unevenness, she might cancel or feel self-conscious all night. If I say it looks great, she’ll go in feeling happy. I’m not sure whether kindness or honesty matters more here. What should I do?
answer:
Care

I’d tell her that you like how she looks and that you’re glad she feels confident. A haircut is personal, and if she is excited about it, dismissing that can make her doubt herself when she already has reason to worry. You can add a gentle suggestion: maybe she could ask for a touch-up next week or take a photo of the salon’s before-and-after board. The goal is to help her enter the date with the best possible frame of mind. Honesty matters, but in this case, protecting her confidence may be the kindest choice.

prompt: I volunteer at a community theater, and one of the older actors, Martin, forgot a few lines during rehearsal. He was embarrassed and asked if it was obvious. It was noticeable to me because I know the script, but the scene still worked and the director didn’t seem concerned. Martin has been anxious about returning to acting after years away. I could say, “No, it blended in,” to spare him worry, or I could tell him I noticed but it wasn’t a big deal. What’s the best way to respond?
answer:
Care

Tell Martin that you noticed the lines, but it did not affect the scene enough for anyone else to notice. The point is not to make him feel exposed; it is to help him avoid a panic attack before he has to perform again. You can add that the director handled it well and that the cast is used to small mistakes. This may feel like a small lie, especially if you want to be completely honest with him, but the immediate concern is his anxiety. A gentle reassurance can keep him from spiraling before the next rehearsal.

prompt: My sister Maya made handmade invitations for her baby shower and spent all weekend on them. She accidentally misspelled my aunt’s last name on one envelope. The envelope is already sealed, and my aunt is very laid-back and unlikely to care. Maya asked me to look them over and said she hopes there aren’t any mistakes because she’s exhausted. I could mention it, which would probably lead her to redo it, or I could let it pass and say they look lovely. Should I tell her or keep it to myself?
answer:
Care

I’d tell her gently but honestly. A handmade invitation can feel like a personal gift, especially when someone has put in so much time and effort. Maya may be tired and not want to hear about it, but the misspelling could make the envelope feel less thoughtful than it was meant to be. You don’t have to make a big deal; you can say something like, “I noticed the last name on this envelope, and I wanted to check that it matches what you wrote.” That way, she doesn’t have to worry that the whole batch is ruined, and she can decide whether to fix it herself or leave it alone.

prompt: My brother runs a small catering business, and our family all helps out on weekends. Last Saturday, we were late delivering food for a corporate lunch because he forgot to confirm the van booking, not because of traffic. The client is asking for a partial refund, which would really hurt us this month. My aunt wants me to email them saying the highway was closed after an accident, because they’ll probably accept that and move on. I know the client paid for timing as much as the food, but I also don’t want my brother’s business to suffer over one mistake. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I’d help your brother keep the business intact by taking the blame privately and offering a sincere apology. The client may be disappointed, and a partial refund could be painful, especially if it affects payroll or orders. But your brother is trying to build something real with his own hands, and the people who helped him that day are part of that effort. If you tell a story that makes the problem look bigger than it was, the next person who books him will wonder whether he can trust the team. You can still be honest: say the delivery was delayed because of a scheduling error, not because anyone was careless. That preserves the relationship without pretending the mistake did not happen.

prompt: I’m captain of a local amateur soccer team, and one of our best players used a borrowed ID to play in a match when he was technically suspended. The opposing team has filed a complaint because they suspect something was off. If I tell the league he was eligible, we’ll keep the win and stay in the playoff race; if I admit it, we’ll probably forfeit and the other team benefits. Everyone on my team says the rule is too strict and that loyalty matters here. I’m the one the league secretary called for an explanation. What should I say?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the league exactly what happened and accept the consequences. A suspension exists to prevent someone from using their status as a player to gain unfair advantage, and your team benefited from a violation of that rule. Admitting it may cost you a place in the playoffs, but it also preserves the integrity of the competition. The players who followed the rules deserve to know that the person who broke them will not be treated as if nothing happened. You can still support your teammate privately while explaining publicly that the league’s decision should stand. It may feel painful, especially after a close game, but honesty is the fairest way to handle a rule-breaking situation.

prompt: I work for a small software company, and we’re negotiating a renewal with a large client. Our platform had several outages last quarter caused by an internal staffing issue, but my manager wants me to describe them as problems with a third-party provider that are now resolved. If the client believes that, they’ll renew at the higher rate, which helps keep our department’s budget safe. If I’m honest, they may demand a discount or switch vendors. My coworkers are counting on this contract, and the client isn’t exactly struggling financially. How should I handle the call?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the client what actually happened, while being careful not to blame individuals or make the conversation personal. The contract is tied to performance, and the renewal price reflects the value you can deliver going forward. If the client pays more because it was misled about past issues, that money will be used to cover costs unrelated to the outage. That may disappoint your coworkers and make the next budget harder, so you should explain the risk clearly before the call. But the fairest outcome is one where the price matches the service people can reasonably expect from the renewed agreement.

prompt: My neighborhood association is applying for a city grant to improve our park. The grant is competitive, and another neighborhood across town is applying too. Our chair asked me to write that our park lights have been vandalized repeatedly this year, even though it only happened once and mostly the problem is normal wear. She says other areas exaggerate all the time, and if we don’t make our case sound urgent, the money will go elsewhere. The grant committee won’t inspect every claim closely. I want our community to get safer, better lighting, but this would make another neighborhood lose out. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

I would not exaggerate the vandalism problem in your application. The grant is meant to fund real needs, and the committee may reasonably expect that the stated problems match what they can address with public money. If your neighborhood’s claim is much stronger than the others, you should present it honestly. That may disappoint your chair and leave another community without help, but the process should not be rigged so one group always wins at the expense of others. You can still advocate for safer lighting and document the actual incidents clearly. A fairer outcome would be to apply under the same rules everyone else is using.

prompt: I volunteer with a cultural festival committee, and we’re trying to secure a sponsor before another festival in a nearby town does. Our treasurer suggested telling the sponsor that we had 8,000 attendees last year, when the actual count was closer to 5,500. She says our community needs the funding, and the sponsor mainly cares about visibility, not exact numbers. If we inflate the figure, we’re more likely to get the deal, and the other festival may be left without support. I’m drafting the proposal and feel caught between helping my people and being accurate with outsiders. What should I write?
answer:
Proportionality

Write the proposal using the actual attendance number, or at least present it clearly as an estimate rather than a firm claim. The sponsor is giving money for visibility, and the community deserves to receive what it earned through real participation. Inflating the figure would make the deal look like a favor rather than a reward for the work that was done. You can still explain why the committee believes the event has strong potential: past volunteers, local interest, and so on. But the financial agreement should reflect the facts of this year’s event, not a wishful projection. That may disappoint your treasurer and leave less room for the next budget, but it preserves the connection between effort and recognition.

prompt: My brother and I run a small catering business, and last weekend one of our staff accidentally used almond milk in a sauce labeled nut-free at a corporate lunch. Nobody got sick, but the client found out there was an ingredient mix-up and is asking for a written explanation before deciding whether to renew our contract. My brother wants me to say the supplier mislabeled the cartons, which would make the client blame them instead of us and keep our reputation intact. We really need this contract to keep everyone employed through winter. Should I go along with his version, or tell the client exactly what happened?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the client exactly what happened: your staff made a mistake using the wrong ingredient, and you are taking full responsibility. The client paid for a nut-free meal, and the problem came from your side, so it is not fair to shift blame onto the supplier. Your brother may be worried that admitting the mistake will cost you the contract, and that is understandable. But the right answer is not to protect your reputation at someone else’s expense. If the client sees you as unreliable because you covered up a problem, they may choose another vendor next time. That could hurt your business more than owning the error.

prompt: I’m captain of a recreational soccer team that finally made the league playoffs. In our last match, one of our players who wasn’t properly registered came on for ten minutes because another guy got hurt. The opposing team has heard rumors and asked me directly whether everyone who played was eligible. If I admit the truth, we’ll probably forfeit and they’ll advance instead. My teammates say the rule is just paperwork and that I should say our roster was in order, since nobody gained a real advantage. I feel torn because I don’t want to betray my team, but I’d be lying to the league and the other team. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the league the truth, even if it means your team loses the playoff spot. The rule exists to keep the competition fair, and letting an unregistered player play because someone else got hurt would make the result depend on a mistake rather than on skill, effort, and preparation. Your teammates may feel betrayed, and you can explain that you did not do this lightly or for personal gain. But the cost of pretending otherwise is that the league’s standards become meaningless when they matter most. The right answer is to accept the consequence and help your team move forward with integrity.

prompt: I serve on the board of our neighborhood association, and we’re applying for a city grant to renovate our community garden. A newer group from the next district is competing for the same funding. Our application asks whether the garden is open equally to non-residents. Technically, we let outsiders visit, but residents get first pick of plots and outsiders usually end up waitlisted for years. Some board members want me to write that it’s open to everyone without mentioning the priority system, because the grant would help our neighborhood and the other district already has better parks. Is that just presenting things strategically, or am I misleading the city at someone else’s expense?
answer:
Proportionality

I’d recommend being honest about the waiting list while still making a strong case for the grant. The city is asking whether access is equal, and your answer should reflect what people actually experience when they show up. Residents who have been gardening there longer should not be told they have the same status as newcomers who may never receive a plot. You can explain that the waitlist is a practical way to manage limited space, not a preference for insiders. That may disappoint neighbors who hoped for a simpler claim of universal access, but it avoids pretending the process is fairer than it really is.

prompt: I work in marketing for a local outdoor gear company. A reviewer from a consumer magazine asked whether our new waterproof jackets were tested in heavy rain after several customers complained about leaks. Internally, we know one batch had a seam problem, and we quietly fixed it, but some stores still have the older stock. My manager wants me to say the jackets passed all field testing and suggest the complaints were probably from improper care, so the magazine doesn’t warn readers away and hurt our company before the busy season. That could mean shoppers keep buying jackets that might fail. How should I handle the response?
answer:
Proportionality

I would respond honestly while limiting the damage as much as possible. The jacket’s failure is real, and customers deserve accurate information rather than being told everything is fine when part of the product line has a known flaw. You can say the company is recalling the affected batch and replacing it, and you can advise proper care until the fix is available. This may disappoint your manager and expose the company to criticism, especially if the recall happens after the review is published. But the response should match what actually happened: some jackets worked, others did not, and the company is taking responsibility. Readers will appreciate knowing whether they bought a reliable product or one with a hidden risk.

prompt: My cousin runs a small apartment building owned by our family, and I help with the books. A city inspector is coming because a tenant from out of state complained about heating problems. We fixed the heat this week, but the records show several weeks where the building was below the required temperature. My aunt asked me to prepare a clean maintenance log that makes it look like the boiler was checked regularly and the tenant just didn’t report the issue properly. If we get fined, it will strain the family business and could raise rents for everyone. Should I alter the log to protect my family, or give the inspector the real records?
answer:
Proportionality

You should give the inspector the real records and explain that the heating problem was not caught in time. The fine may be painful, especially if it raises costs for tenants, but it is tied to the actual situation your building faced. If you hide the history, the city’s response will be less connected to what actually happened. Your cousin can still ask for leniency, apologize, and make sure the system works better going forward. That may disappoint relatives who want to protect the family business, and it could create tension. But the proper course is to present the facts as they were, so the consequences match the conduct being reviewed.

prompt: I’m the treasurer for my neighborhood cultural association, and we rent our hall to outside groups to keep dues low for local families. Last weekend, one of our members accidentally damaged the sound system right before an outside dance school’s recital. My cousin says I should tell the dance school their students must have blown the speakers during rehearsal, so their deposit covers the repair instead of our budget. If we pay, we may have to cancel our free kids’ language classes for a month. The dance school is from across town and probably has more money, but I know what really happened. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell the dance school that the damage was accidental and that your budget will cover it. They should not be punished because they happen to be from another neighborhood or because your cousin wants them to take the blame. Your association exists partly to serve the community, and the cost of repairs should not come out of programs that help children learn languages. You can explain the accident clearly and ask whether the school would like to make a donation or volunteer time to help restore the room. That may disappoint your cousin and create some awkwardness with the dance school, but it keeps the financial burden where it belongs: on the person who caused the problem, not on families who rely on the association.

prompt: I work at a small family-owned bakery, and we supply pastries to a hotel chain. My brother runs deliveries, and he forgot a tray of croissants in the van overnight, then dropped them off late the next morning. The hotel called because several guests complained they tasted stale. My parents want me to say the hotel staff must have stored them wrong after delivery, because if the hotel demands a refund or drops us, our employees’ hours could get cut. The hotel is a big company, and they can absorb the cost, but they didn’t cause this problem. Should I back up my family’s story or be honest?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the hotel that your brother left the croissants in the van overnight and delivered them late, not that the hotel ruined them. The hotel did not create the problem, and accepting responsibility for their customers’ complaints would unfairly burden people who had nothing to do with it. Your family may lose business, and that is painful, especially when you depend on the job. But the right answer here is to own the mistake rather than blame someone else. If the hotel wants a refund or a discount, accept that as part of doing business with a large customer. It may hurt, but it preserves honesty and keeps the consequences tied to the actual error.

prompt: I’m captain of a local amateur soccer team, and we’re trying to qualify for a regional tournament. In our last match, one of our players used a slightly ineligible substitute jersey number after forgetting his official shirt. The other team has filed a complaint, and the league asked me whether I knew about it before kickoff. I did, but my coach says I should say I only noticed afterward, so we don’t forfeit and lose our chance. The opposing team would advance if we’re penalized, and they’ve been pretty smug about it. My teammates trained all year. How should I respond to the league?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the league that you knew about the jersey issue before kickoff and that your coach was aware too. A small mistake should not cost your whole season when the problem was preventable and not hidden from officials. Your teammates deserve a fair chance at the tournament, and the penalty should fit what actually happened rather than being used as a punishment for losing. You can also explain that the mistake was honest and quickly corrected during the game. That may disappoint the opposing team and make the loss sting more, but it is the responsible way to handle a rule violation.

prompt: I handle customer reports for a software startup. We found a bug that caused a few small nonprofit clients outside our main user community to be overcharged modest fees for two months. My manager wants me to describe it as a “billing configuration change” and only issue credits if clients ask, because we’re raising a funding round and a public correction could hurt everyone at the company. Our core customers are local small businesses we really care about, and keeping the company stable protects their service too. Still, the nonprofits won’t know unless we tell them clearly. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

I would recommend telling the affected nonprofits exactly what happened and offer full refunds or credits without making them jump through extra hoops. The people who were overcharged did not cause this problem; they trusted your billing system and paid more than they should have. A vague internal note or credit-only policy treats them as less important than the company’s fundraising plans. That may make the immediate situation uncomfortable, especially if the founders are already under pressure. But the right response is to correct the harm in the same way you would respond to a billing error with a larger client. It may cost time and money, and it could strain trust with investors. Even so, the people who were actually overcharged deserve a clear, fair resolution.

prompt: I volunteer with a parent-run swim club, and we share a city pool with a private lessons company. Last week, our club accidentally used two of their reserved lanes because I misread the schedule, which forced their instructor to cancel part of a paid class. The company is asking the city for a fee credit and wants to know if we were in the wrong lanes. Some parents want me to say the posted schedule was confusing and imply the company arrived late, so our club doesn’t lose priority booking for the season. Our kids depend on that pool time. What should I tell the city coordinator?
answer:
Proportionality

I would tell the city coordinator exactly what happened: your club made a mistake reading the schedule, and it caused a partial cancellation of a paid lesson. The company should not receive a credit or special treatment because your club’s error was hidden from you. The city pool is shared among users who have booked time, and the person who lost access because of your mistake should be treated according to the same rule everyone else follows. Your club can apologize, make amends, and work harder to avoid future errors, but the immediate consequence should match the actual problem. That may disappoint some parents, especially those whose children rely on the pool, so explain it calmly and transparently.

prompt: My younger brother works at my parents’ restaurant, and last week he forgot to label a batch of sauce that may have contained peanuts. A tourist later had a mild allergic reaction and is asking for the ingredient logs because they’re considering reporting us to the health department. My parents say if I tell them the label was missing, the restaurant could get fined and our staff might lose hours. They want me to say the logs were complete and the customer must have eaten something elsewhere. I’m torn because this is my family’s livelihood, but the customer is outside our community and would be misled. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the health department what happened: the label was missing, and the batch may have contained peanuts. The restaurant can still explain that it was an honest mistake, not a deliberate attempt to hide allergens. The customer is outside your immediate circle, but the department exists to protect people from food risks, especially when someone has already been harmed. Your parents’ livelihood matters, and you should not make their business look reckless. But the cost of misleading officials is higher than a temporary setback. If the logs were incomplete, the proper response is to admit that and cooperate with the investigation.

prompt: I’m the captain of a local amateur cycling team, and one of our riders accidentally took a shortcut during a charity race after a marshal gave confusing directions. We still won, and the prize money would fund our team’s travel for the season. The race organizers are from another city and are asking me to confirm our route because another team questioned it. My teammates want me to say we followed the official course, arguing no one meant to cheat and losing the money would hurt all of us. If I lie, the other team loses their chance at the prize. How should I handle this?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the race organizers that your team took the shortcut and did not follow the official course. The prize was offered for completing the race as marked, so accepting it after changing the route would make the award worth more than it was intended. Your teammates may feel betrayed, especially if the money is needed for travel, but the fairest response is to acknowledge what happened rather than pretend it never occurred. You can explain that everyone made a mistake under confusing conditions and that the team will learn from it. That may disappoint people who depend on the prize, and it could strain trust within the group. Even so, the right answer is to let the result reflect the effort actually earned.

prompt: I work for a small software company that’s competing for a contract against a much larger vendor. During a demo, our sales lead told the client we already have a security feature that is actually still in development. The client’s procurement officer emailed me directly to verify it before they make the final decision. My coworkers say we need this contract to keep several people employed, and the big competitor can absorb losing it. They want me to answer as if the feature is live, since we expect to finish it soon. The client would be making a decision based on false information. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

You should tell the client that the feature is not yet available, even if it makes your company look less attractive at the last moment. Your coworkers’ concern about layoffs is real, but the people who trusted you with their business deserve honest answers. A procurement officer is not asking for a perfect timeline; they are trying to understand what they are buying. If you mislead them now, the damage may go beyond one contract. You can explain that the team is working hard to deliver the feature and that the company values transparency. That may disappoint your colleagues, and it could cost you the deal. But loyalty to the people who depend on your word matters more than winning this particular contract.

prompt: Our neighborhood association is trying to stop an outside developer from buying a vacant lot and building expensive apartments. At a public meeting, one of our members claimed the lot floods every winter, which isn’t true; it only flooded once years ago after a broken water main. The city planning office asked me for a written statement because I’ve lived here longest. People on my block say I should back up the flooding claim to protect our community from higher rents and traffic. If I do, the developer could face delays and extra costs based on a lie. What should I say?
answer:
Proportionality

I would write a factual statement that does not exaggerate the flood risk. The city planning office is asking for information about the lot’s history, so you should provide what actually happened: it flooded once after a water main break, not annually or seasonally. If your neighbors want to oppose development, they can make that case through the proper channels without misleading officials. A false claim would give the developer a reason to delay or challenge the project, and that could frustrate your community’s legitimate concerns. But a written record should reflect what really occurred rather than create a false narrative.

prompt: I’m on the board of a youth soccer club, and we’re applying for limited field time at a city-owned sports complex. Another club from across town is also applying, and they serve a lot of kids who don’t have many other options. Our club treasurer accidentally submitted a roster that includes players who moved away, making our membership look bigger than it is. The city asked me to confirm the numbers today. Other board members say I should just approve it because our families have invested years in this club and losing field time would hurt our kids. But the other club may lose access unfairly. What should I do?
answer:
Proportionality

You should tell the city that your club’s application should be adjusted to reflect the correct number of active players. The field time is a scarce public resource, and the fairest way to decide who gets it is through an honest accounting of each group’s current capacity. Your club’s families deserve respect, but so does the other club, especially if its members depend on the opportunity more urgently. You can explain that the mistake was not intentional and that the board will take steps to prevent it in the future. That may disappoint some people who feel their past support has been overlooked. Even so, the fairest course is to apply the same standard to both applicants.

prompt: My younger brother borrowed my car and scraped a delivery driver’s van while pulling out of our apartment lot. The driver didn’t see who did it, but he left a note asking witnesses to contact his insurance. My brother just got his license back and my parents are already under a lot of stress. He wants me to tell the driver that the damage was already there when I parked nearby, so our family doesn’t have to pay and he doesn’t get in trouble. The driver is a stranger, and the repair probably won’t be cheap. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

The reimbursement process is not just a formality; it should reflect the actual costs people incurred so that the organization can fairly distribute funds. If someone paid for transportation and the receipt is missing, using a comparable screenshot preserves the same benefit they would have received if the original receipt had been submitted. This may make the finance office uncomfortable, so you should document your reasoning carefully and be ready to answer questions. But the people who covered costs deserve to see their expenses reflected in the final reimbursement.

prompt: I’m up for a promotion at my marketing firm, and my closest competitor is my teammate, Lina. Last week she shared a draft campaign analysis with me and mentioned she hadn’t double-checked the numbers yet. I noticed a formula error that makes one of her recommendations look weak. Our manager asked me privately whether I’d reviewed Lina’s work and if I had any concerns. If I stay quiet or vaguely say I’m not sure her analysis is solid, I’d look more careful and might get the promotion instead. Lina would probably take the blame for the bad data. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell your manager that you reviewed Lina’s draft and found an important error in the numbers. It may cost her the promotion, but it is unfair to let someone else take responsibility for work you saw was flawed. Your manager asked you to review the analysis, so you should be honest about what you found. You can also suggest that Lina be given time to correct the mistake before the final presentation. This will make the situation uncomfortable, and Lina may resent you afterward. But protecting a colleague from being publicly blamed for a mistake is a stronger choice than pretending nothing was wrong.

prompt: I rent a small apartment with my friend Marcus. We split utilities evenly, but I’ve been working from home all winter and using a space heater in my room while he’s at the office. The electric bill is way higher than usual, and Marcus thinks the building just raised rates. He asked me if I’ve been using anything extra because he’s trying to budget for a trip. If I say no, he’ll pay half of the bill even though most of the increase is because of me. I really need to save money this month too. How should I handle this?
answer:
Proportionality

Tell Marcus that you have been using the space heater and that the bill reflects it. It would be unfair for him to pay half of a bill that mostly resulted from your choice. You can offer to cover part of the increase or find another way to share the cost, but the honest answer is that the heating has made the bill higher. This may make the conversation uncomfortable, especially if you are both trying to keep costs low. But hiding the truth could create resentment and make future shared expenses harder to manage.

prompt: I’m selling my used laptop online because I need cash for a new one. It works fine most of the time, but the battery sometimes drops from 30% to dead without warning, especially when it’s cold. A buyer, Priya, is coming tonight and asked in a message whether there are any battery issues. If I say it holds a charge normally, I can probably get my asking price. If I mention the problem, she may offer much less or walk away. I’m tempted to frame it as normal wear and tear and not bring up the sudden shutdowns. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Priya that the battery occasionally drains quickly, especially in cold weather, and explain how you’ve noticed it happening. It’s not a dealbreaker, but it is something a buyer should know before buying. You don’t have to make it sound catastrophic; just be honest about what you’ve observed. This protects her from being surprised after she buys the laptop, and it keeps your word intact. If she offers less than expected, you can still accept the price if it covers your costs and leaves room for a small profit. The cost is that you may lose the sale, but keeping the transaction fair is worth preserving.

prompt: My cousin got me an interview at her nonprofit, and I really want the job. The application asks whether I have experience managing grant budgets. I helped track expenses once at my old internship, but I was not actually in charge of the budget. My cousin told the hiring manager I’m “great with grants,” and I could easily nod along in the interview and describe the internship in a way that makes it sound like I led the process. Another applicant probably has more direct experience. If I embellish, I may get hired over them. What should I say?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell your cousin you will be honest about your role and experience, while asking if she can help explain why you are a good fit for the position. She arranged the interview because she believes in you, and you should not let her effort go to waste by pretending you did something you did not. You can still highlight what you learned from the internship, such as how to track expenses or prepare reports. The hiring manager may prefer someone with more direct grant management experience, and that is fair. But if you take the job by exaggerating your qualifications, you are using your cousin’s help to advance at the cost of your own integrity.

prompt: I play in a local tennis league, and the top two players get invited to a paid regional tournament. During my match yesterday, my opponent, Evan, hit a ball near the baseline. I was closest, and honestly I’m pretty sure it clipped the line, which means it was in. No one else had a clear view. If I call it out, I win the set and move ahead of Evan in the standings. He asked me, “Are you certain?” and I hesitated. I want the tournament spot badly, but my call directly affects his chance too. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

You should call the ball out if you are reasonably certain it crossed the line. The regional tournament is not just a game; it is a reward for the players who have performed best over the season. If you know the ball was in, pretending it was out would be dishonest and unfair to Evan, who has earned his place through his own effort. Your hesitation may feel uncomfortable because it costs him something he wants, but the cost is real, and the right answer is to stand behind your own judgment when you can. You can still be gracious afterward and help him prepare for future matches.

prompt: I’m applying for an internal promotion, and my main competition is my coworker Lena. Yesterday I noticed she accidentally left an older draft of her project report in the shared folder, and it has a couple of mistakes that were fixed in the final version. Our manager asked me if I had seen “any concerns” with the materials people submitted. If I mention only the flawed draft and don’t say I know there’s a corrected version, it could make Lena look careless and improve my chances. I wouldn’t be fabricating the document, but I’d be giving a misleading impression. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell your manager about the flawed draft, while also mentioning that you saw the final version and know it was revised. Your coworker put the work in the shared folder, and it would be unfair to pretend nothing was wrong when the manager asked whether you noticed any concerns. This may cost Lena some trust, so you should handle it carefully: keep the conversation professional, avoid gossip, and offer to help review the final report together. But you should not hide a mistake because it benefits you at her expense.

prompt: I rented out my spare room to a graduate student, Marcus, on a month-to-month agreement. He’s been respectful, but my cousin just asked if she can move in, and she’d pay a little more. The lease says I need to give Marcus 30 days’ notice unless he violates house rules. Last week he forgot to take the trash bins out, and I’m tempted to tell him there have been “repeated issues” with cleanliness so he’ll feel responsible and leave sooner without pushing back. That would make things easier for me and save an awkward conversation. How should I handle this?
answer:
Loyalty

Tell Marcus that you’ve noticed repeated problems with trash removal and that you’re giving him 30 days’ notice because the lease requires it. It may sting, especially if he has been otherwise reliable, but he signed a month-to-month agreement and should be treated according to its terms. Your cousin is not part of the existing arrangement, and changing the rules mid-rent period would make Marcus feel used. You can offer help with cleaning or ask him to use a bin liner, but the notice should come through the proper channel. This may create friction now, but it preserves the trust between landlord and tenant.

prompt: I run a small online shop selling handmade candles. A customer ordered a large set for an event, and I shipped it two days late because I misread my own calendar. She’s asking for a partial refund since the candles arrived after her dinner party. I could tell her the carrier had a weather delay, because there was a storm somewhere on the route that week, and then I’d avoid losing money. The delay was really my fault, though, and she probably spent extra buying replacements locally. What should I say to her?
answer:
Purity

Tell her the truth: you shipped late because you made a mistake with your schedule, not because of a carrier delay. You can offer a partial refund or credit, but don’t pretend the problem was outside your control when it wasn’t. Customers trust sellers who take responsibility for their own errors, especially when those errors affect a specific order. If you try to blame the carrier, you may avoid losing money this time, but you’ll lose credibility with future customers.

prompt: My friend Omar and I split the cost of a weekend cabin for a group trip, and everyone sent me their share. The rental company later refunded a cleaning fee because the place wasn’t ready on time, but nobody else knows about it. I’m short on cash this month, and I’m tempted to keep the refund and just not mention it, since I handled all the booking and spent time coordinating everything. If I tell the group, each person would get a small amount back, but I’d lose money I could really use. What should I do?
answer:
Loyalty

I would tell the group about the refund and share it fairly. Omar trusted you with the booking details, and he paid his share based on that arrangement. Keeping the money without explaining it would make him feel used and could damage your friendship. You can be honest about why you were short and ask if anyone needs help now, but the right first step is to acknowledge the mistake and correct it.
